\subsection{Espressif (ESP32 chip series)}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/espressif:espressif-esp32-chip-series}}\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/espressif::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL can be used and configured as a standard \sphinxhref{https://github.com/espressif/esp-idf}{ESP\sphinxhyphen{}IDF} component.

\sphinxAtStartPar
More information about ESP\sphinxhyphen{}IDF build system can be found \sphinxhref{https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/latest/esp32/api-guides/build-system.html}{here}.


\subsubsection{LVGL demo project for ESP32}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/espressif:lvgl-demo-project-for-esp32}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We've created \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lv\_port\_esp32}{lv\_port\_esp32}, a project using ESP\sphinxhyphen{}IDF and LVGL to show one of the demos from \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/demos}{demos}.
You can configure the project to use one of the many supported display controllers and targets (chips).

\sphinxAtStartPar
See \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl\_esp32\_drivers}{lvgl\_esp32\_drivers} repository for a complete list
of supported display and indev (touch) controllers and targets.


\subsubsection{Using LVGL in your ESP\sphinxhyphen{}IDF project}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/espressif:using-lvgl-in-your-esp-idf-project}}

\paragraph{Prerequisites}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/espressif:prerequisites}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ESP\sphinxhyphen{}IDF v4.1 and above

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ESP evaluation board with a display

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Obtaining LVGL}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/espressif:obtaining-lvgl}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Option 1:} git submodule

\sphinxAtStartPar
Simply clone LVGL into your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{project\_root/components}} directory and it will be automatically integrated into the project.
If the project is a git repository you can include LVGL as a git submodule:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git submodule add https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl.git components/lvgl
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The above command will clone LVGL's main repository into the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{components/lvgl}} directory. LVGL includes a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeLists.txt}} file that sets some configuration options so you can use LVGL right away.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Option 2:} IDF Component Manager

\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL is also distributed through \sphinxhref{https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/latest/esp32/api-guides/tools/idf-component-manager.html}{IDF Component Manager}.
It allows users to seamlessly integrate \sphinxhref{https://components.espressif.com/component/lvgl/lvgl}{LVGL component} into their project with following command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
idf.py add\PYGZhy{}dependency lvgl/lvgl\PYGZgt{}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{8}.*
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
During next project build, LVGL component will be fetched from the component registry and added to project build.


\paragraph{Configuration}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/espressif:configuration}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When you are ready to configure LVGL, launch the configuration menu with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{idf.py menuconfig}} in your project root directory, go to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Component config}} and then \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LVGL configuration}}.


\subsubsection{Using lvgl\_esp32\_drivers in ESP\sphinxhyphen{}IDF project}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/espressif:using-lvgl-esp32-drivers-in-esp-idf-project}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also add \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl\_esp32\_drivers}} as a "component". This component should be located inside a directory named "components" in your project root directory.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When your project is a git repository you can include \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl\_esp32\_drivers}} as a git submodule:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git submodule add https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl\PYGZus{}esp32\PYGZus{}drivers.git components/lvgl\PYGZus{}esp32\PYGZus{}drivers
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Renesas}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/renesas:renesas}}\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/renesas::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://bit.ly/3I9nfUo}{HMI\sphinxhyphen{}Board} development board SDK now comes with LVGL integration for quick evaluation. Simply download the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/RT-Thread-Studio/sdk-bsp-ra6m3-hmi-board/tree/main/projects/hmi-board-lvgl}{SDK} for the supported motherboard and you’ll be on your way to creating your next GUI application in no time. For more information, check out the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/RT-Thread-Studio/sdk-bsp-ra6m3-hmi-board/blob/main/projects/hmi-board-lvgl/README}{Software design description}.


\subsubsection{Creating new project with LVGL}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/renesas:creating-new-project-with-lvgl}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is recommended to start your project by downloading the HMI\sphinxhyphen{}Board SDK example project. It comes fully equipped with LVGL and dave\sphinxhyphen{}2d support (if the modules are present), so you won’t need to do any additional integration work.


\subsubsection{HW acceleration for Renesas RA6M3 platforms}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/renesas:hw-acceleration-for-renesas-ra6m3-platforms}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For RA6M3 platforms, hardware acceleration can be achieved using the dave\sphinxhyphen{}2d GPU, depending on the platform used. Each accelerator has its own context, allowing them to be used individually or simultaneously in LVGL’s multithreading mode.


\paragraph{Dave\sphinxhyphen{}2d accelerator}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/renesas:dave-2d-accelerator}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL can offload several drawing features to the dave\sphinxhyphen{}2d engine, freeing up the CPU for other operations while dave\sphinxhyphen{}2d runs. An RTOS is required to block the LVGL drawing thread and switch to another task or suspend the CPU for power savings. Supported draw callbacks can be found in “src/draw/renesas/lv\_gpu\_d2\_ra6m3.c”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL can offload several drawing features to the dave\sphinxhyphen{}2d engine, freeing up the CPU for other operations while dave\sphinxhyphen{}2d runs. An RTOS is required to block the LVGL drawing thread and switch to another task or suspend the CPU for power savings. Supported draw callbacks can be found in “src/draw/renesas/lv\_gpu\_d2\_ra6m3.c”.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
	\PYG{n}{ra\PYGZus{}2d\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{blend} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ra6m3\PYGZus{}2d\PYGZus{}blend}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{ra\PYGZus{}2d\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{base\PYGZus{}draw}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoded} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}port\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoded}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{ra\PYGZus{}2d\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{base\PYGZus{}draw}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{wait\PYGZus{}for\PYGZus{}finish} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}port\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}wait}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{ra\PYGZus{}2d\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{base\PYGZus{}draw}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}letter} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}letter}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Features supported:}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/renesas:features-supported}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{All} \PYG{n}{operations} \PYG{n}{can} \PYG{n}{be} \PYG{n}{used} \PYG{n}{in} \PYG{n}{conjunction} \PYG{n}{with} \PYG{n}{optional} \PYG{n}{transparency}\PYG{p}{.}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
RGB565 and ARGB8888 color formats

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Area fill with color

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
BLIT (BLock Image Transfer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Color conversion

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rotate and scale

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Alpha blending

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bilinear filtering

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
RTOS integration layer

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Default RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread code provided

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Subpixel exact placement

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Basic configuration:}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/renesas:basic-configuration}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Select Renesas dave\sphinxhyphen{}2d engine in lv\_conf.h: Set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_USE\_GPU\_RA6M3\_G2D}} to 1

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set referenced header file in lv\_conf.h: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#define LV\_GPU\_RA6M3\_G2D\_INCLUDE "hal\_data.h"}}

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread Example:}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/renesas:rt-thread-example}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{define COLOR\PYGZus{}BUFFER  (LV\PYGZus{}HOR\PYGZus{}RES\PYGZus{}MAX * LV\PYGZus{}VER\PYGZus{}RES\PYGZus{}MAX)}

\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*A static or global variable to store the buffers*/}
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}color\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}1}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{COLOR\PYGZus{}BUFFER}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
After initializing your peripherals (such as SPI, GPIOs, and LCD) in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_port\_disp\_init()}} function, you can initialize LVGL using \sphinxhref{https://docs.lvgl.io/master/API/core/lv\_obj.html\#\_CPPv47lv\_initv}{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_init()}}.} Next, register the frame buffers using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_draw\_buf\_init()}} and create a new display driver using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_init()}}.

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/*Initialize `disp\PYGZus{}buf` with the buffer(s). With only one buffer use NULL instead buf\PYGZus{}2 */}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}buf\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}buf}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{RT\PYGZus{}NULL}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{COLOR\PYGZus{}BUFFER}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{c+cm}{/*Basic initialization*/}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set the resolution of the display*/}
\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{hor\PYGZus{}res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}HOR\PYGZus{}RES\PYGZus{}MAX}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{ver\PYGZus{}res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}VER\PYGZus{}RES\PYGZus{}MAX}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set a display buffer*/}
\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}buf} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}buf}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Used to copy the buffer\PYGZsq{}s content to the display*/}
\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{flush\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}flush}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/* Initialize GPU module */}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}port\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}hw\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Finally register the driver*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}register}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
To run LVGL, you’ll need to create a thread. You can find examples of how to do this using RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{env\_support/rt\sphinxhyphen{}thread/lv\_rt\_thread\_port.c}} file.

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{lvgl\PYGZus{}thread\PYGZus{}entry}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{parameter}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{if LV\PYGZus{}USE\PYGZus{}LOG}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}log\PYGZus{}register\PYGZus{}print\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}rt\PYGZus{}log}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{endif }\PYG{c+cm}{/* LV\PYGZus{}USE\PYGZus{}LOG */}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}port\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}port\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}user\PYGZus{}gui\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

    \PYG{c+cm}{/* handle the tasks of LVGL */}
    \PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
        \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}task\PYGZus{}handler}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{n}{rt\PYGZus{}thread\PYGZus{}mdelay}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}DISP\PYGZus{}DEF\PYGZus{}REFR\PYGZus{}PERIOD}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{k+kt}{int} \PYG{n+nf}{lvgl\PYGZus{}thread\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{n}{rt\PYGZus{}err\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{err}\PYG{p}{;}
	
    \PYG{c+cm}{/* create lvgl thread */}
    \PYG{n}{err} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{rt\PYGZus{}thread\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}thread}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{LVGL}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}thread\PYGZus{}entry}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{RT\PYGZus{}NULL}\PYG{p}{,}
           \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}thread\PYGZus{}stack}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{sizeof}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}thread\PYGZus{}stack}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{PKG\PYGZus{}LVGL\PYGZus{}THREAD\PYGZus{}PRIO}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{err} \PYG{o}{!}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{RT\PYGZus{}EOK}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
        \PYG{n}{LOG\PYGZus{}E}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Failed to create LVGL thread}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{l+m+mi}{\PYGZhy{}1}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
    \PYG{n}{rt\PYGZus{}thread\PYGZus{}startup}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}thread}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

    \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{n}{INIT\PYGZus{}ENV\PYGZus{}EXPORT}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}thread\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {}

\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{my\PYGZus{}flush\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{const} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}area\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{area}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}color\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{color\PYGZus{}p}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{ifdef PKG\PYGZus{}USING\PYGZus{}ILI9341}

\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{else}

    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}flush\PYGZus{}ready}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\subsection{Arduino}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/arduino:arduino}}\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/arduino::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl}{LVGL library} is directly available as Arduino libraries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that you need to choose a board powerful enough to run LVGL and your GUI.  See the \sphinxhref{https://docs.lvgl.io/master/intro/index.html\#requirements}{requirements of LVGL}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example ESP32 is a good candidate to create UI's with LVGL.


\subsubsection{Get the LVGL Arduino library}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/arduino:get-the-lvgl-arduino-library}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL can be installed via the Arduino IDE Library Manager or as a .ZIP library.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/archive/refs/heads/master.zip}{Download} the latest version of LVGL from GitHub and simply copy it to Arduino's library folder.


\subsubsection{Set up drivers}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/arduino:set-up-drivers}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To get started it's recommended to use \sphinxhref{https://github.com/Bodmer/TFT\_eSPI}{TFT\_eSPI} library as a TFT driver to simplify testing.
To make it work, setup \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TFT\_eSPI}} according to your TFT display type via editing either
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{User\_Setup.h}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
or by selecting a configuration in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{User\_Setup\_Select.h}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Both files are located in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TFT\_eSPI}} library's folder.


\subsubsection{Configure LVGL}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/arduino:configure-lvgl}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL has its own configuration file called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}}. When LVGL is installed, follow these configuration steps:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Go to the directory of the installed Arduino libraries

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Go to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl}} and copy \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf\_template.h}} as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} into the Arduino Libraries directory next to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl}} library folder.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} and change the first \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#if 0}} to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#if 1}} to enable the content of the file

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the color depth of you display in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_COLOR\_DEPTH}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_TICK\_CUSTOM 1}}

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally the layout with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} should look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{arduino}
 \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{libraries}
   \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl}
   \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{other\PYGZus{}lib\PYGZus{}1}
   \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{other\PYGZus{}lib\PYGZus{}2}
   \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}conf}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{h}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Initialize and run LVGL}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/arduino:initialize-and-run-lvgl}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Take a look at \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/blob/master/examples/arduino/LVGL\_Arduino/LVGL\_Arduino.ino}{LVGL\_Arduino.ino} to see how to initialize LVGL.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TFT\_eSPI}} is used as the display driver.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the INO file you can see how to register a display and a touchpad for LVGL and call an example.


\subsubsection{Use the examples and demos}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/arduino:use-the-examples-and-demos}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that, there is no dedicated INO file for every example. Instead, you can load an example by calling an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_example\_...}} function. For example \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_example\_btn\_1()}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{IMPORTANT NOTE 1}
Due to some the limitations of Arduino's build system you need to copy \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl/examples}} to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl/src/examples}}. Similarly for the demos \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl/demos}} to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl/src/demos}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{IMPORTANT NOTE 2}
Note that the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_examples}} library is for LVGL v7 and you shouldn't install it for this version (since LVGL v8)
as the examples and demos are now part of the main LVGL library.


\subsubsection{Debugging and logging}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/arduino:debugging-and-logging}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL can display debug information in case of trouble.
In the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LVGL\_Arduino.ino}} example there is a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{my\_print}} method, which sends this debug information to the serial interface.
To enable this feature you have to edit the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} file and enable logging in the section \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{log settings}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/*Log settings*/}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{define USE\PYGZus{}LV\PYGZus{}LOG      1   }\PYG{c+cm}{/*Enable/disable the log module*/}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{if LV\PYGZus{}USE\PYGZus{}LOG}
\PYG{c+cm}{/* How important log should be added:}
\PYG{c+cm}{ * LV\PYGZus{}LOG\PYGZus{}LEVEL\PYGZus{}TRACE       A lot of logs to give detailed information}
\PYG{c+cm}{ * LV\PYGZus{}LOG\PYGZus{}LEVEL\PYGZus{}INFO        Log important events}
\PYG{c+cm}{ * LV\PYGZus{}LOG\PYGZus{}LEVEL\PYGZus{}WARN        Log if something unwanted happened but didn\PYGZsq{}t cause a problem}
\PYG{c+cm}{ * LV\PYGZus{}LOG\PYGZus{}LEVEL\PYGZus{}ERROR       Only critical issue, when the system may fail}
\PYG{c+cm}{ * LV\PYGZus{}LOG\PYGZus{}LEVEL\PYGZus{}NONE        Do not log anything}
\PYG{c+cm}{ */}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{  define LV\PYGZus{}LOG\PYGZus{}LEVEL    LV\PYGZus{}LOG\PYGZus{}LEVEL\PYGZus{}WARN}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After enabling the log module and setting LV\_LOG\_LEVEL accordingly, the output log is sent to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Serial}} port @ 115200 bps.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Tasmota and berry}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/tasmota-berry:tasmota-and-berry}}\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/tasmota-berry::doc}}

\subsubsection{What is Tasmota?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/tasmota-berry:what-is-tasmota}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/arendst/Tasmota}{Tasmota} is a widely used open\sphinxhyphen{}source firmware for ESP8266 and EPS32 based devices. It supports a wide variety of devices, sensors and integrations to Home Automation and Cloud services. Tasmota firmware is downloaded more than 200,000 times each month, and has an active and growing community.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tasmota provides access to hundreds of supported devices, full support of MQTT, HTTP(S), integration with major Home Automation systems, myriad of sensors, IR, RF, Zigbee, Bluetooth, AWS IoT, Azure IoT, Alexa and many more.


\subsubsection{What is Berry?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/tasmota-berry:what-is-berry}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/berry-lang/berry}{Berry} is a ultra\sphinxhyphen{}lightweight dynamically typed embedded scripting language. It is designed for lower\sphinxhyphen{}performance embedded devices. The interpreter of Berry include a one\sphinxhyphen{}pass compiler and register\sphinxhyphen{}based VM, all the code is written in ANSI C99. Berry offers a syntax very similar to Python, and is inspired from LUA VM. It is fully integrated in Tasmota


\paragraph{Highlights of Berry}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/tasmota-berry:highlights-of-berry}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Berry has the following advantages:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Lightweight: A well\sphinxhyphen{}optimized interpreter with very little resources. Ideal for use in microprocessors.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fast: optimized one\sphinxhyphen{}pass bytecode compiler and register\sphinxhyphen{}based virtual machine.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Powerful: supports imperative programming, object\sphinxhyphen{}oriented programming, functional programming.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Flexible: Berry is a dynamic type script, and it's intended for embedding in applications. It can provide good dynamic scalability for the host system.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Simple: simple and natural syntax, support garbage collection, and easy to use FFI (foreign function interface).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
RAM saving: With compile\sphinxhyphen{}time object construction, most of the constant objects are stored in read\sphinxhyphen{}only code data segments, so the RAM usage of the interpreter is very low when it starts.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All features are detailed in the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/berry-lang/berry/wiki/Reference}{Berry Reference Manual}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Why LVGL + Tasmota + Berry?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/tasmota-berry:why-lvgl-tasmota-berry}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In 2021, Tasmota added full support of LVGL for ESP32 based devices. It also introduced the Berry scripting language, a small\sphinxhyphen{}footprint language similar to Python and fully integrated in Tasmota.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A comprehensive mapping of LVGL in Berry language is now available, similar to the mapping of Micropython. It allows to use +98\% of all LVGL features. It is also possible to write custom widgets in Berry.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Versions supported: LVGL v8.3.0, LodePNG v20201017, Freetype 2.10.4


\paragraph{Tasmota + Berry + LVGL could be used for:}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/tasmota-berry:tasmota-berry-lvgl-could-be-used-for}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fast prototyping GUI.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Shortening the cycle of changing and fine\sphinxhyphen{}tuning the GUI.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Modelling the GUI in a more abstract way by defining reusable composite objects, taking advantage of Berry's language features such as Inheritance, Closures, Exception Handling...

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Make LVGL accessible to a larger audience. No need to know C to create a nice GUI on an embedded system.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A higher level interface compatible with \sphinxhref{https://github.com/HASwitchPlate/openHASP}{OpenHASP} is also under development.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{So what does it look like?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/tasmota-berry:so-what-does-it-look-like}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
TL;DR:
Similar to MicroPython, it's very much like the C API, but Object\sphinxhyphen{}Oriented for LVGL components.
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let's dive right into an example!


\paragraph{A simple example}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/tasmota-berry:a-simple-example}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{start}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}                 \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} start LVGL}
\PYG{n}{scr} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{scr\PYGZus{}act}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}         \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} get default screen}
\PYG{n}{btn} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{btn}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{scr}\PYG{p}{)}          \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} create button}
\PYG{n}{btn}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{center}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{label} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{label}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{btn}\PYG{p}{)}      \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} create a label in the button}
\PYG{n}{label}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}text}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Button}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}   \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} set a label to the button}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{How can I use it?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/tasmota-berry:how-can-i-use-it}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can start in less than 10 minutes on a M5Stack or equivalent device in less than 10 minutes in this \sphinxhref{https://tasmota.github.io/docs/LVGL\_in\_10\_minutes/}{short tutorial}

\subsection{CMake}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/cmake:cmake}}\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/cmake::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL supports integrating with \sphinxhref{https://cmake.org/}{CMake}. It comes with preconfigured targets for:

\sphinxAtStartPar
On top of the preconfigured targets you can also use "plain" CMake to integrate LVGL into any custom C/C++ project.


\subsubsection{Prerequisites}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/cmake:prerequisites}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
CMake ( >= 3.12.4 )

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compatible build tool e.g.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Building LVGL with CMake}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/cmake:building-lvgl-with-cmake}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are many ways to include external CMake projects into your own. A modern one also used in this example is the CMake \sphinxhref{https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/FetchContent.html}{FetchContent} module. This module conveniently allows us to download dependencies directly at configure time from e.g. \sphinxhref{https://github.com/}{GitHub}. Here is an example how we might include LVGL into our own project.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cmake\PYGZus{}minimum\PYGZus{}required}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{VERSION} \PYG{l+s}{3.14}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{include}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{FetchContent}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n+nb}{project}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{MyProject} \PYG{l+s}{LANGUAGES} \PYG{l+s}{C} \PYG{l+s}{CXX}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} Build an executable called \PYGZdq{}MyFirmware\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{n+nb}{add\PYGZus{}executable}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{MyFirmware} \PYG{l+s}{src/main.c}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} Specify path to own LVGL config header}
\PYG{n+nb}{set}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{LV\PYGZus{}CONF\PYGZus{}PATH}
    \PYG{o}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{CMAKE\PYGZus{}CURRENT\PYGZus{}SOURCE\PYGZus{}DIR}\PYG{o}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s}{/src/lv\PYGZus{}conf.h}
    \PYG{l+s}{CACHE} \PYG{l+s}{STRING} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}} \PYG{l+s}{FORCE}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} Fetch LVGL from GitHub}
\PYG{n+nb}{FetchContent\PYGZus{}Declare}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{lvgl} \PYG{l+s}{URL} \PYG{l+s}{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl.git}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{FetchContent\PYGZus{}MakeAvailable}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{lvgl}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} The target \PYGZdq{}MyFirmware\PYGZdq{} depends on LVGL}
\PYG{n+nb}{target\PYGZus{}link\PYGZus{}libraries}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{MyFirmware} \PYG{l+s}{PRIVATE} \PYG{l+s}{lvgl::lvgl}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This configuration declares a dependency between the two targets \sphinxstylestrong{MyFirmware} and \sphinxstylestrong{lvgl}. Upon building the target \sphinxstylestrong{MyFirmware} this dependency will be resolved and \sphinxstylestrong{lvgl} will be built and linked with it. Since LVGL requires a config header called \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/blob/master/lv\_conf\_template.h}{lv\_conf.h} to be includable by its sources we also set the option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_CONF\_PATH}} to point to our own copy of it.


\paragraph{Additional CMake options}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/cmake:additional-cmake-options}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Besides \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_CONF\_PATH}} there are two additional CMake options to specify include paths.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LVGL\_H\_INCLUDE\_SIMPLE}} which specifies whether to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#include "lvgl.h"}} absolut or relative



\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_CONF\_INCLUDE\_SIMPLE}} which specifies whether to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#include "lv\_conf.h"}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"lv\_drv\_conf.h"}} absolut or relative



\sphinxAtStartPar
I do not recommend disabling those options unless your folder layout makes it absolutely necessary.


\subsubsection{Building LVGL examples with CMake}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/cmake:building-lvgl-examples-with-cmake}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL \sphinxhref{https://docs.lvgl.io/master/examples.html}{examples} have their own CMake target. If you want to build the examples simply add them to your dependencies.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} The target \PYGZdq{}MyFirmware\PYGZdq{} depends on LVGL and examples}
\PYG{n+nb}{target\PYGZus{}link\PYGZus{}libraries}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{MyFirmware} \PYG{l+s}{PRIVATE} \PYG{l+s}{lvgl::lvgl} \PYG{l+s}{lvgl::examples}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Building LVGL drivers and demos with CMake}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/cmake:building-lvgl-drivers-and-demos-with-cmake}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Exactly the same goes for the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lv\_drivers}{drivers} and the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/demos}{demos}.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{FetchContent\PYGZus{}Declare}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{lv\PYGZus{}drivers}
                     \PYG{l+s}{GIT\PYGZus{}REPOSITORY} \PYG{l+s}{https://github.com/lvgl/lv\PYGZus{}drivers}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{FetchContent\PYGZus{}MakeAvailable}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{lv\PYGZus{}drivers}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} The target \PYGZdq{}MyFirmware\PYGZdq{} depends on LVGL, drivers and demos}
\PYG{n+nb}{target\PYGZus{}link\PYGZus{}libraries}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{MyFirmware} \PYG{l+s}{PRIVATE} \PYG{l+s}{lvgl::lvgl} \PYG{l+s}{lvgl::drivers} \PYG{l+s}{lvgl::examples}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Build shared libraries with CMake}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/platforms/cmake:build-shared-libraries-with-cmake}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, LVGL will be built as a static library (archive). CMake can instead be instructed to build LVGL as shared library (.so/.dll/etc.):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{set}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{BUILD\PYGZus{}SHARED\PYGZus{}LIBS} \PYG{l+s}{ON}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
OR

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{\PYGZdl{}} \PYG{n}{cmake} \PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZhy{}DBUILD\PYGZus{}SHARED\PYGZus{}LIBS=ON}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}} \PYG{p}{.}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{(RT)OS}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/index:rt-os}}\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/index::doc}}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{NuttX RTOS}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:nuttx-rtos}}\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx::doc}}

\subsubsection{What is NuttX?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:what-is-nuttx}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://nuttx.apache.org/}{NuttX} is a mature and secure real\sphinxhyphen{}time operating system (RTOS) with an emphasis on technical standards compliance and small size.
It is scalable from 8\sphinxhyphen{}bit to 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit microcontrollers and microprocessors and compliant with the Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) standards and with many Linux\sphinxhyphen{}like subsystems.
The best way to think about NuttX is to think of it as a small Unix/Linux for microcontrollers.


\paragraph{Highlights of NuttX}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:highlights-of-nuttx}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Small} \sphinxhyphen{} Fits and runs in microcontrollers as small as 32 kB Flash and 8 kB of RAM.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Compliant} \sphinxhyphen{} Strives to be as compatible as possible with POSIX and Linux.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Versatile} \sphinxhyphen{} Supports many architectures (ARM, ARM Thumb, AVR, MIPS, OpenRISC, RISC\sphinxhyphen{}V 32\sphinxhyphen{}bit and 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit, RX65N, x86\sphinxhyphen{}64, Xtensa, Z80/Z180, etc.).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Modular} \sphinxhyphen{} Its modular design allows developers to select only what really matters and use modules to include new features.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Popular} \sphinxhyphen{} NuttX is used by many companies around the world. Probably you already used a product with NuttX without knowing it was running NuttX.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Predictable} \sphinxhyphen{} NuttX is a preemptible Realtime kernel, so you can use it to create predictable applications for realtime control.

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Why NuttX + LVGL?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:why-nuttx-lvgl}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Although NuttX has its own graphic library called \sphinxhref{https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=139629474}{NX}, LVGL is a good alternative because users could find more eye\sphinxhyphen{}candy demos and they can reuse code from previous projects.
LVGL is an \sphinxhref{https://blog.lvgl.io/2018-12-13/extend-lvgl-objects}{Object\sphinxhyphen{}Oriented Component Based} high\sphinxhyphen{}level GUI library, that could fit very well for a RTOS with advanced features like NuttX.
LVGL is implemented in C and its APIs are in C.


\paragraph{Here are some advantages of using LVGL in NuttX}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:here-are-some-advantages-of-using-lvgl-in-nuttx}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Develop GUI in Linux first and when it is done just compile it for NuttX. Nothing more, no wasting of time.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually, GUI development for low level RTOS requires multiple iterations to get things right, where each iteration consists of \sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Change code}} > \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Build}} > \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Flash}} > \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Run}}}.
Using LVGL, Linux and NuttX you can reduce this process and just test everything on your computer and when it is done, compile it on NuttX and that is it.

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{NuttX + LVGL could be used for}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:nuttx-lvgl-could-be-used-for}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
GUI demos to demonstrate your board graphics capacities.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fast prototyping GUI for MVP (Minimum Viable Product) presentation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
visualize sensor data directly and easily on the board without using a computer.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Final products with a GUI without a touchscreen (i.e. 3D Printer Interface using Rotary Encoder to Input data).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Final products with a touchscreen (and all sorts of bells and whistles).

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{How to get started with NuttX and LVGL?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:how-to-get-started-with-nuttx-and-lvgl}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are many boards in the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/apache/incubator-nuttx}{NuttX mainline} with support for LVGL.
Let's use the \sphinxhref{https://www.st.com/en/evaluation-tools/32f429idiscovery.html}{STM32F429IDISCOVERY} as an example because it is a very popular board.


\paragraph{First you need to install the pre\sphinxhyphen{}requisites on your system}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:first-you-need-to-install-the-pre-requisites-on-your-system}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let's use the \sphinxhref{https://acassis.wordpress.com/2018/01/10/how-to-build-nuttx-on-windows-10/}{Windows Subsystem for Linux}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} sudo apt\PYGZhy{}get install automake bison build\PYGZhy{}essential flex gcc\PYGZhy{}arm\PYGZhy{}none\PYGZhy{}eabi gperf git libncurses5\PYGZhy{}dev libtool libusb\PYGZhy{}dev libusb\PYGZhy{}1.0.0\PYGZhy{}dev pkg\PYGZhy{}config kconfig\PYGZhy{}frontends openocd
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Now let's create a workspace to save our files}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:now-let-s-create-a-workspace-to-save-our-files}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} mkdir \PYGZti{}/nuttxspace
\PYGZdl{} \PYG{n+nb}{cd} \PYGZti{}/nuttxspace
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Clone the NuttX and Apps repositories:}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:clone-the-nuttx-and-apps-repositories}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} git clone https://github.com/apache/incubator\PYGZhy{}nuttx nuttx
\PYGZdl{} git clone https://github.com/apache/incubator\PYGZhy{}nuttx\PYGZhy{}apps apps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Configure NuttX to use the stm32f429i\sphinxhyphen{}disco board and the LVGL Demo}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:configure-nuttx-to-use-the-stm32f429i-disco-board-and-the-lvgl-demo}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} ./tools/configure.sh stm32f429i\PYGZhy{}disco:lvgl
\PYGZdl{} make
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If everything went fine you should have now the file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nuttx.bin}} to flash on your board:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} ls \PYGZhy{}l nuttx.bin
\PYGZhy{}rwxrwxr\PYGZhy{}x \PYG{l+m}{1} alan alan \PYG{l+m}{287144} Jun \PYG{l+m}{27} \PYG{l+m}{09}:26 nuttx.bin
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Flashing the firmware in the board using OpenOCD:}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/nuttx:flashing-the-firmware-in-the-board-using-openocd}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} sudo openocd \PYGZhy{}f interface/stlink\PYGZhy{}v2.cfg \PYGZhy{}f target/stm32f4x.cfg \PYGZhy{}c init \PYGZhy{}c \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}reset halt\PYGZdq{}} \PYGZhy{}c \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}flash write\PYGZus{}image erase nuttx.bin 0x08000000\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reset the board and using the 'NSH>' terminal start the LVGL demo:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
nsh\PYGZgt{} lvgldemo
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsection{RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread RTOS}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/rt-thread:rt-thread-rtos}}\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/rt-thread::doc}}



\subsubsection{What is RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/rt-thread:what-is-rt-thread}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k7QYk6hSwnc}{Introduce about RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread and how to run LVGL on RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread in simulators}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://www.rt-thread.io/}{\sphinxstylestrong{RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread}} is an \sphinxhref{https://github.com/RT-Thread/rt-thread}{open source}, neutral, and community\sphinxhyphen{}based real\sphinxhyphen{}time operating system (RTOS). RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread has \sphinxstylestrong{Standard version} and \sphinxstylestrong{Nano version}. For resource\sphinxhyphen{}constrained microcontroller (MCU) systems, the Nano version that requires only 3 KB Flash and 1.2 KB RAM memory resources can be tailored with easy\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}use tools. For resource\sphinxhyphen{}rich IoT devices, RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread can use the \sphinxstylestrong{online software package} management tool, together with system configuration tools, to achieve intuitive and rapid modular cutting, seamlessly import rich software packages; thus, achieving complex functions like Android's graphical interface and touch sliding effects, smart voice interaction effects, and so on.


\paragraph{Key features}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/rt-thread:key-features}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Designed for resource\sphinxhyphen{}constrained devices, the minimum kernel requires only 1.2KB of RAM and 3 KB of Flash.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A variety of standard interfaces, such as POSIX, CMSIS, C++ application environment.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Has rich components and a prosperous and fast growing package ecosystem

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Elegant code style, easy to use, read and master.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
High Scalability. RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread has high\sphinxhyphen{}quality scalable software architecture, loose coupling, modularity, is easy to tailor and expand.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Supports high\sphinxhyphen{}performance applications.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Supports all mainstream compiling tools such as GCC, Keil and IAR.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Supports a wide range of architectures and chips.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{How to run LVGL on RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/rt-thread:how-to-run-lvgl-on-rt-thread}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://www.rt-thread.org/document/site/\#/rt-thread-version/rt-thread-standard/packages-manual/lvgl-docs/introduction}{中文文档}

\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL has registered as a \sphinxhref{https://packages.rt-thread.org/en/detail.html?package=LVGL}{software package} of RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread. By using \sphinxhref{https://www.rt-thread.io/download.html?download=Env}{Env tool} or \sphinxhref{https://www.rt-thread.io/download.html?download=Studio}{RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread Studio IDE}, RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread users can easily download LVGL source code and combine with RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread project. RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread community has port LVGL to several BSPs:




\paragraph{Import a BSP project into RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread Studio}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/os/rt-thread:import-a-bsp-project-into-rt-thread-studio}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Clone the latest code from RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread official repository. Open the RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread Studio and select \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{File \sphinxhyphen{}> Import}}. In the Import menu, please select \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread BSP Project into Workspace}}, and click \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{next}} button. In the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BSP location area}}, please select the root path of the BSP which you prefer to import, such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C:\textbackslash{}Users\textbackslash{}xxx\textbackslash{}Desktop\textbackslash{}rt\sphinxhyphen{}thread\textbackslash{}bsp\textbackslash{}stm32\textbackslash{}stm32l475\sphinxhyphen{}atk\sphinxhyphen{}pandora}}. In the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Project Name area}}, please type a name for this project, then, press \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Finish}} button.

\subsection{Micropython}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:micropython}}\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython::doc}}

\subsubsection{What is Micropython?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:what-is-micropython}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{http://micropython.org/}{Micropython} is Python for microcontrollers.
Using Micropython, you can write Python3 code and run it even on a bare metal architecture with limited resources.


\paragraph{Highlights of Micropython}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:highlights-of-micropython}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Compact} \sphinxhyphen{} Fits and runs within just 256k of code space and 16k of RAM. No OS is needed, although you can also run it with an OS, if you want.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Compatible} \sphinxhyphen{} Strives to be as compatible as possible with normal Python (known as CPython).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Versatile} \sphinxhyphen{} Supports many architectures (x86, x86\sphinxhyphen{}64, ARM, ARM Thumb, Xtensa).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interactive} \sphinxhyphen{} No need for the compile\sphinxhyphen{}flash\sphinxhyphen{}boot cycle. With the REPL (interactive prompt) you can type commands and execute them immediately, run scripts, etc.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Popular} \sphinxhyphen{} Many platforms are supported. The user base is growing bigger. Notable forks: \sphinxhref{https://github.com/micropython/micropython}{MicroPython}, \sphinxhref{https://github.com/adafruit/circuitpython}{CircuitPython}, \sphinxhref{https://github.com/loboris/MicroPython\_ESP32\_psRAM\_LoBo}{MicroPython\_ESP32\_psRAM\_LoBo}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Embedded Oriented} \sphinxhyphen{} Comes with modules specifically for embedded systems, such as the \sphinxhref{https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/library/machine.html\#classes}{machine module} for accessing low\sphinxhyphen{}level hardware (I/O pins, ADC, UART, SPI, I2C, RTC, Timers etc.)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Why Micropython + LVGL?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:why-micropython-lvgl}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, Micropython \sphinxhref{https://forum.micropython.org/viewtopic.php?f=18\&t=5543}{does not have a good high\sphinxhyphen{}level GUI library} by default. LVGL is an \sphinxhref{https://blog.lvgl.io/2018-12-13/extend-lvgl-objects}{Object\sphinxhyphen{}Oriented Component Based} high\sphinxhyphen{}level GUI library, which seems to be a natural candidate to map into a higher level language, such as Python. LVGL is implemented in C and its APIs are in C.


\paragraph{Here are some advantages of using LVGL in Micropython:}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:here-are-some-advantages-of-using-lvgl-in-micropython}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Develop GUI in Python, a very popular high level language. Use paradigms such as Object\sphinxhyphen{}Oriented Programming.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually, GUI development requires multiple iterations to get things right. With C, each iteration consists of \sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Change code}} > \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Build}} > \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Flash}} > \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Run}}}.
In Micropython it's just \sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Change code}} > \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Run}}} ! You can even run commands interactively using the \sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Read\%E2\%80\%93eval\%E2\%80\%93print\_loop}{REPL} (the interactive prompt)

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Micropython + LVGL could be used for:}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:micropython-lvgl-could-be-used-for}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fast prototyping GUI.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Shortening the cycle of changing and fine\sphinxhyphen{}tuning the GUI.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Modelling the GUI in a more abstract way by defining reusable composite objects, taking advantage of Python's language features such as Inheritance, Closures, List Comprehension, Generators, Exception Handling, Arbitrary Precision Integers and others.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Make LVGL accessible to a larger audience. No need to know C to create a nice GUI on an embedded system.
This goes well with \sphinxhref{https://learn.adafruit.com/welcome-to-circuitpython/what-is-circuitpython}{CircuitPython vision}. CircuitPython was designed with education in mind, to make it easier for new or inexperienced users to get started with embedded development.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Creating tools to work with LVGL at a higher level (e.g. drag\sphinxhyphen{}and\sphinxhyphen{}drop designer).

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{So what does it look like?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:so-what-does-it-look-like}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
TL;DR:
It's very much like the C API, but Object\sphinxhyphen{}Oriented for LVGL components.
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let's dive right into an example!


\paragraph{A simple example}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:a-simple-example}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{lvgl} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{lv}
\PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{scr} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{obj}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{btn} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{btn}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{scr}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{btn}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{align}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{scr\PYGZus{}act}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{ALIGN}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{CENTER}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{label} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{label}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{btn}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{label}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}text}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Button}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{lv}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{scr\PYGZus{}load}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{scr}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{How can I use it?}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:how-can-i-use-it}}

\paragraph{Online Simulator}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:online-simulator}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to experiment with LVGL + Micropython without downloading anything \sphinxhyphen{} you can use our online simulator!
It's a fully functional LVGL + Micropython that runs entirely in the browser and allows you to edit a python script and run it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://sim.lvgl.io/}{Click here to experiment on the online simulator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://sim.lvgl.io/v7/micropython/ports/javascript/bundle\_out/index.html?script=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/amirgon/51299ce9b6448328a855826149482ae6/raw/0f235c6d40462fd2f0e55364b874f14fe3fd613c/lvgl\_hello\_world.py\&script\_startup=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/amirgon/7bf15a66ba6d959bbf90d10f3da571be/raw/8684b5fa55318c184b1310663b187aaab5c65be6/init\_lv\_mp\_js.py}{Hello World}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note: the online simulator is available for lvgl v6 and v7.


\paragraph{PC Simulator}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:pc-simulator}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Micropython is ported to many platforms. One notable port is "unix", which allows you to build and run Micropython (+LVGL) on a Linux machine. (On a Windows machine you might need Virtual Box or WSL or MinGW or Cygwin etc.)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lv\_micropython}{Click here to know more information about building and running the unix port}


\paragraph{Embedded platform}
\label{\detokenize{get-started/bindings/micropython:embedded-platform}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the end, the goal is to run it all on an embedded platform.
Both Micropython and LVGL can be used on many embedded architectures, such as stm32, ESP32 etc.
You would also need display and input drivers. We have some sample drivers (ESP32+ILI9341, as well as some other examples), but chances are you would want to create your own input/display drivers for your specific hardware.
Drivers can be implemented either in C as a Micropython module, or in pure Micropython!

\chapter{Porting}
\label{\detokenize{porting/index:porting}}\label{\detokenize{porting/index::doc}}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{Set up a project}
\label{\detokenize{porting/project:set-up-a-project}}\label{\detokenize{porting/project::doc}}

\subsection{Get the library}
\label{\detokenize{porting/project:get-the-library}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL is available on GitHub: \sphinxurl{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can clone it or \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/archive/refs/heads/master.zip}{Download} the latest version of the library from GitHub.


\subsection{Add lvgl to your project}
\label{\detokenize{porting/project:add-lvgl-to-your-project}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The graphics library itself is the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl}} directory. It contains a couple of folders but to use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl}} you only need \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.c}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.h}} files from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}} folder.


\subsubsection{Automatically add files}
\label{\detokenize{porting/project:automatically-add-files}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If your IDE automatically adds the files from the folders copied to the project folder (as Eclipse or VSCode does), you can simply copy the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl}} folder as it is into your project.


\subsubsection{Make and CMake}
\label{\detokenize{porting/project:make-and-cmake}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL also supports \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMake}} build systems out of the box. To add LVGL to your Makefile based build system add these lines to your main Makefile:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{LVGL\PYGZus{}DIR\PYGZus{}NAME} \PYG{o}{?=} lvgl     \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}The name of the lvgl folder (change this if you have renamed it)}
\PYG{n+nv}{LVGL\PYGZus{}DIR} \PYG{o}{?=} \PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{shell}\PYG{p}{ pwd}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}The path where the lvgl folder is}
\PYG{c+cp}{include \PYGZdl{}(LVGL\PYGZus{}DIR)/\PYGZdl{}(LVGL\PYGZus{}DIR\PYGZus{}NAME)/lvgl.mk}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For integration with CMake take a look this section of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{get-started/platforms/cmake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Documentation}}}}.


\subsubsection{Other platforms and tools}
\label{\detokenize{porting/project:other-platforms-and-tools}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{/get-started/index.html}{Get started} section contains many platform specific descriptions e.g. for ESP32, Arduino, NXP, RT\sphinxhyphen{}Thread, NuttX, etc.


\subsubsection{Demos and Examples}
\label{\detokenize{porting/project:demos-and-examples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl}} folder also contains an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples}} and a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{demos}} folder. If you needed to add the source files manually to your project, you can do the same with the source files of these two folders too. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMake}} handles the examples and demos, so no extra action required in these cases.


\subsection{Configuration file}
\label{\detokenize{porting/project:configuration-file}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There is a configuration header file for LVGL called \sphinxstylestrong{lv\_conf.h}. You modify this header to set the library's basic behavior, disable unused modules and features, adjust the size of memory buffers in compile\sphinxhyphen{}time, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To get \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} \sphinxstylestrong{copy lvgl/lv\_conf\_template.h} next to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl}} directory and rename it to \sphinxstyleemphasis{lv\_conf.h}. Open the file and change the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#if 0}} at the beginning to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#if 1}} to enable its content. So the layout of the files should look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl}
\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}conf}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{h}
\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{other} \PYG{n}{files} \PYG{n}{and} \PYG{n}{folders}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Comments in the config file explain the meaning of the options. Be sure to set at least \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_COLOR\_DEPTH}} according to your display's color depth. Note that, the examples and demos explicitly need to be enabled in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternatively, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} can be copied to another place but then you should add the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_CONF\_INCLUDE\_SIMPLE}} define to your compiler options (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLV\_CONF\_INCLUDE\_SIMPLE}} for GCC compiler) and set the include path manually (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}I../include/gui}}).
In this case LVGL will attempt to include \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} simply with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#include "lv\_conf.h"}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can even use a different name for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}}. The custom path can be set via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_CONF\_PATH}} define.
For example \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLV\_CONF\_PATH="/home/joe/my\_project/my\_custom\_conf.h"}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_CONF\_SKIP}} is defined, LVGL will not try to include \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}}. Instead you can pass the config defines using build options. For example \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"\sphinxhyphen{}DLV\_COLOR\_DEPTH=32 \sphinxhyphen{}DLV\_USE\_BTN=1"}}. The unset options will get a default value which is the same as the ones in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf\_template.h}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL also can be used via \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Kconfig}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{menuconfig}}.  You can use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} together with Kconfig, but keep in mind that the value from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} or build settings (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D...}}) overwrite the values set in Kconfig. To ignore the configs from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} simply remove its content, or define \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_CONF\_SKIP}}.


\subsection{Initialization}
\label{\detokenize{porting/project:initialization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To use the graphics library you have to initialize it and setup required components. The order of the initialization is:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_init()}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Initialize your drivers.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Register the display and input devices drivers in LVGL.  Learn more about {\hyperref[\detokenize{porting/display::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Display}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{porting/indev::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Input device}}}} registration.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_tick\_inc(x)}} every \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{x}} milliseconds in an interrupt to report the elapsed time to LVGL. {\hyperref[\detokenize{porting/tick::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Learn more}}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler()}} every few milliseconds to handle LVGL related tasks. {\hyperref[\detokenize{porting/timer-handler::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Learn more}}}}.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Display interface}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:display-interface}}\label{\detokenize{porting/display::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To register a display for LVGL, a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_draw\_buf\_t}} and a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_t}} variable have to be initialized.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_draw\_buf\_t}} contains internal graphic buffer(s) called draw buffer(s).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_t}} contains callback functions to interact with the display and manipulate low level drawing behavior.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Draw buffer}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:draw-buffer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Draw buffer(s) are simple array(s) that LVGL uses to render the screen content.
Once rendering is ready the content of the draw buffer is sent to the display using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flush\_cb}} function set in the display driver (see below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
A draw buffer can be initialized via a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_draw\_buf\_t}} variable like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/*A static or global variable to store the buffers*/}
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}buf\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}buf}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Static or global buffer(s). The second buffer is optional*/}
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}color\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}1}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{MY\PYGZus{}DISP\PYGZus{}HOR\PYGZus{}RES} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}color\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}2}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{MY\PYGZus{}DISP\PYGZus{}HOR\PYGZus{}RES} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Initialize `disp\PYGZus{}buf` with the buffer(s). With only one buffer use NULL instead buf\PYGZus{}2 */}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}buf\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}buf}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}2}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{MY\PYGZus{}DISP\PYGZus{}HOR\PYGZus{}RES}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_draw\_buf\_t}} must be a static, global or dynamically allocated variable. It cannot be a local variable as they are destroyed upon end of scope.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As you can see above, the draw buffer may be smaller than the screen. In this case, larger areas are redrawn in smaller segments that fit into the draw buffer(s).
If only a small area changes (e.g. a button is pressed) then only that area will be refreshed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A larger buffer results in better performance but above 1/10 screen sized buffer(s) there is no significant performance improvement.
Therefore it's recommended to choose the size of the draw buffer(s) to be at least 1/10 screen sized.


\subsection{Buffering modes}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:buffering-modes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are several settings to adjust the number draw buffers and buffering/refreshing modes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can measure the performance of different configurations using the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/tree/master/demos/benchmark}{benchmark example}.


\subsubsection{One buffer}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:one-buffer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If only one buffer is used LVGL draws the content of the screen into that draw buffer and sends it to the display.
LVGL then needs to wait until the content of the buffer is sent to the display before drawing something new in it.


\subsubsection{Two buffers}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:two-buffers}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If two buffers  are used LVGL can draw into one buffer while the content of the other buffer is sent to the display in the background.
DMA or other hardware should be used to transfer data to the display so the MCU can continue drawing.
This way, the rendering and refreshing of the display become parallel operations.


\subsubsection{Full refresh}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:full-refresh}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the display driver (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_t}}) enabling the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{full\_refresh}} bit will force LVGL to always redraw the whole screen. This works in both \sphinxstyleemphasis{one buffer} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{two buffers} modes.
If \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{full\_refresh}} is enabled and two screen sized draw buffers are provided, LVGL's display handling works like "traditional" double buffering.
This means the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flush\_cb}} callback only has to update the address of the framebuffer (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{color\_p}} parameter).
This configuration should be used if the MCU has an LCD controller peripheral and not with an external display controller (e.g. ILI9341 or SSD1963) accessed via serial link. The latter will generally be too slow to maintain high frame rates with full screen redraws.


\subsubsection{Direct mode}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:direct-mode}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{direct\_mode}} flag is enabled in the display driver LVGL will draw directly into a \sphinxstylestrong{screen sized frame buffer}. That is the draw buffer(s) needs to be screen sized.
It this case \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flush\_cb}} will be called only once when all dirty areas are redrawn.
With \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{direct\_mode}} the frame buffer always contains the current frame as it should be displayed on the screen.
If 2 frame buffers are provided as draw buffers LVGL will alter the buffers but always draw only the dirty areas.
Therefore the 2 buffers needs to synchronized in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flush\_cb}} like this:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Display the frame buffer pointed by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{color\_p}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Copy the redrawn areas from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{color\_p}} to the other buffer.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The get the redrawn areas to copy use the following functions
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_lv\_refr\_get\_disp\_refreshing()}} returns the display being refreshed
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{disp\sphinxhyphen{}>inv\_areas{[}LV\_INV\_BUF\_SIZE{]}}} contains the invalidated areas
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{disp\sphinxhyphen{}>inv\_area\_joined{[}LV\_INV\_BUF\_SIZE{]}}} if 1 that area was joined into another one and should be ignored
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{disp\sphinxhyphen{}>inv\_p}} number of valid elements in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{inv\_areas}}


\subsection{Display driver}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:display-driver}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Once the buffer initialization is ready a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_t}} display driver needs to be:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
initialized with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_init(\&disp\_drv)}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
its fields need to be set

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
it needs to be registered in LVGL with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_register(\&disp\_drv)}}

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_t}} also needs to be a static, global or dynamically allocated variable.


\subsubsection{Mandatory fields}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:mandatory-fields}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the most simple case only the following fields of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_t}} need to be set:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_buf}} pointer to an initialized \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_draw\_buf\_t}} variable.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{hor\_res}} horizontal resolution of the display in pixels.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ver\_res}} vertical resolution of the display in pixels.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flush\_cb}} a callback function to copy a buffer's content to a specific area of the display.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_flush\_ready(\&disp\_drv)}} needs to be called when flushing is ready.
LVGL might render the screen in multiple chunks and therefore call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flush\_cb}} multiple times. To see if the current one is the last chunk of rendering use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_flush\_is\_last(\&disp\_drv)}}.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Optional fields}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:optional-fields}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are some optional display driver data fields:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{physical\_hor\_res}} horizontal resolution of the full / physical display in pixels. Only set this when \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} using the full screen (defaults to \sphinxhyphen{}1 / same as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{hor\_res}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{physical\_ver\_res}} vertical resolution of the full / physical display in pixels. Only set this when \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} using the full screen (defaults to \sphinxhyphen{}1 / same as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ver\_res}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{offset\_x}} horizontal offset from the full / physical display in pixels. Only set this when \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} using the full screen (defaults to 0).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{offset\_y}} vertical offset from the full / physical display in pixels. Only set this when \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} using the full screen (defaults to 0).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{color\_chroma\_key}} A color which will be drawn as transparent on chrome keyed images. Set to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_COLOR\_CHROMA\_KEY}} from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} by default.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{anti\_aliasing}} use anti\sphinxhyphen{}aliasing (edge smoothing). Enabled by default if \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_COLOR\_DEPTH}} is set to at least 16 in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rotated}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sw\_rotate}} See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{porting/display:rotation}]{\emph{Rotation}}} section below.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{screen\_transp}} if \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1}} the screen itself can have transparency as well. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_COLOR\_SCREEN\_TRANSP}} must be enabled in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_COLOR\_DEPTH}} must be 32.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{user\_data}} A custom \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void}} user data for the driver.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{full\_refresh}} always redrawn the whole screen (see above)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{direct\_mode}} draw directly into the frame buffer (see above)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some other optional callbacks to make it easier and more optimal to work with monochrome, grayscale or other non\sphinxhyphen{}standard RGB displays:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rounder\_cb}} Round the coordinates of areas to redraw. E.g. a 2x2 px can be converted to 2x8.
It can be used if the display controller can refresh only areas with specific height or width (usually 8 px height with monochrome displays).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{set\_px\_cb}} a custom function to write the draw buffer. It can be used to store the pixels more compactly in the draw buffer if the display has a special color format. (e.g. 1\sphinxhyphen{}bit monochrome, 2\sphinxhyphen{}bit grayscale etc.)
This way the buffers used in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_draw\_buf\_t}} can be smaller to hold only the required number of bits for the given area size. Note that rendering with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{set\_px\_cb}} is slower than normal rendering.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{monitor\_cb}} A callback function that tells how many pixels were refreshed and in how much time. Called when the last chunk is rendered and sent to the display.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clean\_dcache\_cb}} A callback for cleaning any caches related to the display.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{render\_start\_cb}} A callback function that notifies the display driver that rendering has started. It also could be used to wait for VSYNC to start rendering. It's useful if rendering is faster than a VSYNC period.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL has built\sphinxhyphen{}in support to several GPUs (see \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}}) but if something else is required these functions can be used to make LVGL use a GPU:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gpu\_fill\_cb}} fill an area in the memory with a color.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gpu\_wait\_cb}} if any GPU function returns while the GPU is still working, LVGL will use this function when required to make sure GPU rendering is ready.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:examples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All together it looks like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{;}          \PYG{c+cm}{/*A variable to hold the drivers. Must be static or global.*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}            \PYG{c+cm}{/*Basic initialization*/}
\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}buf} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}buf}\PYG{p}{;}          \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set an initialized buffer*/}
\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{flush\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}flush\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}        \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set a flush callback to draw to the display*/}
\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{hor\PYGZus{}res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{320}\PYG{p}{;}                 \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set the horizontal resolution in pixels*/}
\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{ver\PYGZus{}res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{240}\PYG{p}{;}                 \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set the vertical resolution in pixels*/}

\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{disp}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{disp} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}register}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{c+cm}{/*Register the driver and save the created display objects*/}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are some simple examples of the callbacks:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{my\PYGZus{}flush\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{const} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}area\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{area}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}color\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{color\PYGZus{}p}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{c+cm}{/*The most simple case (but also the slowest) to put all pixels to the screen one\PYGZhy{}by\PYGZhy{}one}
\PYG{c+cm}{     *`put\PYGZus{}px` is just an example, it needs to implemented by you.*/}
    \PYG{k+kt}{int32\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{y}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{k}{for}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{y} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{y1}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{n}{y} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{y2}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{n}{y}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
        \PYG{k}{for}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{x} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{x1}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{n}{x} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{x2}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{n}{x}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
            \PYG{n}{put\PYGZus{}px}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{y}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{color\PYGZus{}p}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
            \PYG{n}{color\PYGZus{}p}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

    \PYG{c+cm}{/* IMPORTANT!!!}
\PYG{c+cm}{     * Inform the graphics library that you are ready with the flushing*/}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}flush\PYGZus{}ready}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{my\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}fill\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}color\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{dest\PYGZus{}buf}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{const} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}area\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{dest\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{const} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}area\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{fill\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}color\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{color}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{c+cm}{/*It\PYGZsq{}s an example code which should be done by your GPU*/}
    \PYG{k+kt}{uint32\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{y}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{dest\PYGZus{}buf} \PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{dest\PYGZus{}width} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{fill\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{y1}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{c+cm}{/*Go to the first line*/}

    \PYG{k}{for}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{y} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{fill\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{y1}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{n}{y} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}} \PYG{n}{fill\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{y2}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{n}{y}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
        \PYG{k}{for}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{x} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{fill\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{x1}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{n}{x} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}} \PYG{n}{fill\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{x2}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{n}{x}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
