\subsection{Other options}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:other-options}}

\subsubsection{Rotation}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:rotation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL supports rotation of the display in 90 degree increments. You can select whether you'd like software rotation or hardware rotation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you select software rotation (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sw\_rotate}} flag set to 1), LVGL will perform the rotation for you. Your driver can and should assume that the screen width and height have not changed. Simply flush pixels to the display as normal. Software rotation requires no additional logic in your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flush\_cb}} callback.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is a noticeable amount of overhead to performing rotation in software. Hardware rotation is available to avoid unwanted slowdowns. In this mode, LVGL draws into the buffer as if your screen width and height were swapped. You are responsible for rotating the provided pixels yourself.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default rotation of your display when it is initialized can be set using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rotated}} flag. The available options are \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_DISP\_ROT\_NONE}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_DISP\_ROT\_90}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_DISP\_ROT\_180}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_DISP\_ROT\_270}}. The rotation values are relative to how you would rotate the physical display in the clockwise direction. Thus, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_DISP\_ROT\_90}} means you rotate the hardware 90 degrees clockwise, and the display rotates 90 degrees counterclockwise to compensate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
(Note for users upgrading from 7.10.0 and older: these new rotation enum values match up with the old 0/1 system for rotating 90 degrees, so legacy code should continue to work as expected. Software rotation is also disabled by default for compatibility.)

\sphinxAtStartPar
Display rotation can also be changed at runtime using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_set\_rotation(disp, rot)}} API.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you enable rotation the coordinates of the pointer input devices (e.g. touchpad) will be rotated too.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that when using software rotation, you cannot use neither \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{direct\_mode}} nor \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{full\_refresh}} in the driver. When using either of these, you will have to rotate the pixels yourself e.g. in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flush\_cb}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Support for software rotation is a new feature, so there may be some glitches/bugs depending on your configuration. If you encounter a problem please open an issue on \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/issues}{GitHub}.


\subsubsection{Decoupling the display refresh timer}
\label{\detokenize{porting/display:decoupling-the-display-refresh-timer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Normally the dirty (a.k.a invalid) areas are checked and redrawn in every \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_DISP\_DEF\_REFR\_PERIOD}} milliseconds (set in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}}).
However, in some cases you might need more control on when the display refreshing happen, for example to synchronize rendering with VSYNC or the TE signal.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can do this in the following way:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/*Delete the original display refresh timer*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}timer\PYGZus{}del}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{disp}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{refr\PYGZus{}timer}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{disp}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{refr\PYGZus{}timer} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{;}


\PYG{c+cm}{/*Call this anywhere you want to refresh the dirty areas*/}
\PYG{n}{\PYGZus{}lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}refr\PYGZus{}timer}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have multiple displays call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_set\_deafult(disp1);}} to select the display to refresh before \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_lv\_disp\_refr\_timer(NULL);}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler()}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_lv\_disp\_refr\_timer()}} can not run at the same time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the performance monitor is enabled, the value of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_DISP\_DEF\_REFR\_PERIOD}} needs to be set to be consistent with the refresh period of the display to ensure that the statistical results are correct.

\section{Input device interface}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:input-device-interface}}\label{\detokenize{porting/indev::doc}}

\subsection{Types of input devices}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:types-of-input-devices}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To register an input device an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_indev\_drv\_t}} variable has to be initialized. \sphinxstylestrong{Be sure to register at least one display before you register any input devices.}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/*Register at least one display before you register any input devices*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}register}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{disp\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}      \PYG{c+cm}{/*Basic initialization*/}
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{type} \PYG{o}{=}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}                 \PYG{c+cm}{/*See below.*/}
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}              \PYG{c+cm}{/*See below.*/}
\PYG{c+cm}{/*Register the driver in LVGL and save the created input device object*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}indev} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}register}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{type}} member can be:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_INDEV\_TYPE\_POINTER}} touchpad or mouse

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_INDEV\_TYPE\_KEYPAD}} keyboard or keypad

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_INDEV\_TYPE\_ENCODER}} encoder with left/right turn and push options

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_INDEV\_TYPE\_BUTTON}} external buttons virtually pressing the screen

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{read\_cb}} is a function pointer which will be called periodically to report the current state of an input device.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Visit {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/indev::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Input devices}}}} to learn more about input devices in general.


\subsubsection{Touchpad, mouse or any pointer}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:touchpad-mouse-or-any-pointer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Input devices that can click points on the screen belong to this category.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{type} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}TYPE\PYGZus{}POINTER}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}input\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}

\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}input\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}data\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{touchpad\PYGZus{}pressed}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{point}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{x} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{touchpad\PYGZus{}x}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{point}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{y} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{touchpad\PYGZus{}y}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{state} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}STATE\PYGZus{}PRESSED}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}} \PYG{k}{else} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{state} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}STATE\PYGZus{}RELEASED}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To set a mouse cursor use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_indev\_set\_cursor(my\_indev, \&img\_cursor)}}. (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{my\_indev}} is the return value of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_indev\_drv\_register}})


\subsubsection{Keypad or keyboard}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:keypad-or-keyboard}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Full keyboards with all the letters or simple keypads with a few navigation buttons belong here.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use a keyboard/keypad:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Register a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{read\_cb}} function with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_INDEV\_TYPE\_KEYPAD}} type.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
An object group has to be created: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_group\_t * g = lv\_group\_create()}} and objects have to be added to it with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_group\_add\_obj(g, obj)}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The created group has to be assigned to an input device: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_indev\_set\_group(my\_indev, g)}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{my\_indev}} is the return value of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_indev\_drv\_register}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_KEY\_...}} to navigate among the objects in the group. See \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_core/lv\_group.h}} for the available keys.

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{type} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}TYPE\PYGZus{}KEYPAD}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{keyboard\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}

\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n}{keyboard\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}data\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{key} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{last\PYGZus{}key}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}            \PYG{c+cm}{/*Get the last pressed or released key*/}

  \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{key\PYGZus{}pressed}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{state} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}STATE\PYGZus{}PRESSED}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{k}{else} \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{state} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}STATE\PYGZus{}RELEASED}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Encoder}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:encoder}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With an encoder you can do the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Press its button

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Long\sphinxhyphen{}press its button

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Turn left

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Turn right

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In short, the Encoder input devices work like this:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
By turning the encoder you can focus on the next/previous object.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When you press the encoder on a simple object (like a button), it will be clicked.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you press the encoder on a complex object (like a list, message box, etc.) the object will go to edit mode whereby you can navigate inside the object by turning the encoder.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
To leave edit mode, long press the button.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Encoder} (similarly to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Keypads}) the objects should be added to groups.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{type} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}TYPE\PYGZus{}ENCODER}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{encoder\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}

\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n}{encoder\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}data\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{enc\PYGZus{}diff} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{enc\PYGZus{}get\PYGZus{}new\PYGZus{}moves}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

  \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{enc\PYGZus{}pressed}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{state} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}STATE\PYGZus{}PRESSED}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{k}{else} \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{state} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}STATE\PYGZus{}RELEASED}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Using buttons with Encoder logic}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:using-buttons-with-encoder-logic}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to standard encoder behavior, you can also utilize its logic to navigate(focus) and edit widgets using buttons.
This is especially handy if you have only few buttons available, or you want to use other buttons in addition to encoder wheel.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You need to have 3 buttons available:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_KEY\_ENTER}} will simulate press or pushing of the encoder button

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_KEY\_LEFT}} will simulate turning encoder left

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_KEY\_RIGHT}} will simulate turning encoder right

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
other keys will be passed to the focused widget

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you hold the keys it will simulate an encoder advance with period specified in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{indev\_drv.long\_press\_repeat\_time}}.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{type} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}TYPE\PYGZus{}ENCODER}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{encoder\PYGZus{}with\PYGZus{}keys\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}

\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n}{encoder\PYGZus{}with\PYGZus{}keys\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}data\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{key} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{last\PYGZus{}key}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}            \PYG{c+cm}{/*Get the last pressed or released key*/}
                                     \PYG{c+cm}{/* use LV\PYGZus{}KEY\PYGZus{}ENTER for encoder press */}
  \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{key\PYGZus{}pressed}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{state} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}STATE\PYGZus{}PRESSED}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{k}{else} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
      \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{state} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}STATE\PYGZus{}RELEASED}\PYG{p}{;}
      \PYG{c+cm}{/* Optionally you can also use enc\PYGZus{}diff, if you have encoder*/}
      \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{enc\PYGZus{}diff} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{enc\PYGZus{}get\PYGZus{}new\PYGZus{}moves}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Button}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:button}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Buttons} mean external "hardware" buttons next to the screen which are assigned to specific coordinates of the screen.
If a button is pressed it will simulate the pressing on the assigned coordinate. (Similarly to a touchpad)

\sphinxAtStartPar
To assign buttons to coordinates use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_indev\_set\_button\_points(my\_indev, points\_array)}}.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{points\_array}} should look like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{const lv\_point\_t points\_array{[}{]} = \{ \{12,30\},\{60,90\}, ...\}}}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The points\_array can't go out of scope. Either declare it as a global variable or as a static variable inside a function.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{type} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}INDEV\PYGZus{}TYPE\PYGZus{}BUTTON}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{indev\PYGZus{}drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{button\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}

\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n}{button\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}indev\PYGZus{}data\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}

\subsection{Other features}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:other-features}}

\subsubsection{Parameters}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:parameters}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default value of the following parameters can be changed in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_indev\_drv\_t}}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scroll\_limit}} Number of pixels to slide before actually scrolling the object.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scroll\_throw}}  Scroll throw (momentum) slow\sphinxhyphen{}down in {[}\%{]}. Greater value means faster slow\sphinxhyphen{}down.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{long\_press\_time}} Press time to send \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_EVENT\_LONG\_PRESSED}} (in milliseconds)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{long\_press\_repeat\_time}} Interval of sending \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_EVENT\_LONG\_PRESSED\_REPEAT}} (in milliseconds)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{read\_timer}} pointer to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer}} which reads the input device. Its parameters can be changed by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_...()}} functions. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_INDEV\_DEF\_READ\_PERIOD}} in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} sets the default read period.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Feedback}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:feedback}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Besides \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{read\_cb}} a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{feedback\_cb}} callback can be also specified in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_indev\_drv\_t}}.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{feedback\_cb}} is called when any type of event is sent by the input devices (independently of its type). This allows generating feedback for the user, e.g. to play a sound on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_EVENT\_CLICKED}}.


\subsubsection{Associating with a display}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:associating-with-a-display}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Every input device is associated with a display. By default, a new input device is added to the last display created or explicitly selected (using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_set\_default()}}).
The associated display is stored and can be changed in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{disp}} field of the driver.


\subsubsection{Buffered reading}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:buffered-reading}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, LVGL calls \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{read\_cb}} periodically. Because of this intermittent polling there is a chance that some user gestures are missed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To solve this you can write an event driven driver for your input device that buffers measured data. In \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{read\_cb}} you can report the buffered data instead of directly reading the input device.
Setting the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data\sphinxhyphen{}>continue\_reading}} flag will tell LVGL there is more data to read and it should call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{read\_cb}} again.


\subsection{Further reading}
\label{\detokenize{porting/indev:further-reading}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/blob/master/examples/porting/lv\_port\_indev\_template.c}{lv\_port\_indev\_template.c} for a template for your own driver.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/display::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{INdev features}}}} to learn more about higher level input device features.

\end{itemize}

\section{Tick interface}
\label{\detokenize{porting/tick:tick-interface}}\label{\detokenize{porting/tick::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL needs a system tick to know elapsed time for animations and other tasks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You need to call the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_tick\_inc(tick\_period)}} function periodically and provide the call period in milliseconds. For example, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_tick\_inc(1)}} when calling every millisecond.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_tick\_inc}} should be called in a higher priority routine than \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_task\_handler()}} (e.g. in an interrupt) to precisely know the elapsed milliseconds even if the execution of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_task\_handler}} takes more time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With FreeRTOS \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_tick\_inc}} can be called in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vApplicationTickHook}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On Linux based operating systems (e.g. on Raspberry Pi) \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_tick\_inc}} can be called in a thread like below:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n+nf}{tick\PYGZus{}thread} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
      \PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
        \PYG{n}{usleep}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1000}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}   \PYG{c+cm}{/*Sleep for 5 millisecond*/}
        \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}tick\PYGZus{}inc}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}      \PYG{c+cm}{/*Tell LVGL that 5 milliseconds were elapsed*/}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{API}
\label{\detokenize{porting/tick:api}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Provide access to the system tick with 1 millisecond resolution

\section{Timer Handler}
\label{\detokenize{porting/timer-handler:timer-handler}}\label{\detokenize{porting/timer-handler::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To handle the tasks of LVGL you need to call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler()}} periodically in one of the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{while(1)} of \sphinxstyleemphasis{main()} function

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
timer interrupt periodically (lower priority than \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_tick\_inc()}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
an OS task periodically

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The timing is not critical but it should be about 5 milliseconds to keep the system responsive.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}timer\PYGZus{}handler}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}delay\PYGZus{}ms}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler()}} in a super\sphinxhyphen{}loop, a helper function\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler\_run\_in\_period()}} is provided to simplify the porting:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}timer\PYGZus{}handler\PYGZus{}run\PYGZus{}in\PYGZus{}period}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{c+cm}{/* run lv\PYGZus{}timer\PYGZus{}handler() every 5ms */}
    \PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In an OS environment, you can use it together with the \sphinxstylestrong{delay} or \sphinxstylestrong{sleep} provided by OS to release CPU whenever possible:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{while} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}timer\PYGZus{}handler\PYGZus{}run\PYGZus{}in\PYGZus{}period}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{c+cm}{/* run lv\PYGZus{}timer\PYGZus{}handler() every 5ms */}
    \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}delay\PYGZus{}ms}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}                    \PYG{c+cm}{/* delay 5ms to avoid unnecessary polling */}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To learn more about timers visit the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/timer::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Timer}}}} section.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Sleep management}
\label{\detokenize{porting/sleep:sleep-management}}\label{\detokenize{porting/sleep::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The MCU can go to sleep when no user input happens. In this case, the main \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{while(1)}} should look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Normal operation (no sleep) in \PYGZlt{} 1 sec inactivity*/}
  \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}get\PYGZus{}inactive\PYGZus{}time}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1000}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
	  \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}task\PYGZus{}handler}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Sleep after 1 sec inactivity*/}
  \PYG{k}{else} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
	  \PYG{n}{timer\PYGZus{}stop}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}   \PYG{c+cm}{/*Stop the timer where lv\PYGZus{}tick\PYGZus{}inc() is called*/}
	  \PYG{n}{sleep}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}		    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Sleep the MCU*/}
  \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
  \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}delay\PYGZus{}ms}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You should also add the following lines to your input device read function to signal a wake\sphinxhyphen{}up (press, touch or click etc.) has happened:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}tick\PYGZus{}inc}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}DISP\PYGZus{}DEF\PYGZus{}REFR\PYGZus{}PERIOD}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Force task execution on wake\PYGZhy{}up*/}
\PYG{n}{timer\PYGZus{}start}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}                         \PYG{c+cm}{/*Restart the timer where lv\PYGZus{}tick\PYGZus{}inc() is called*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}task\PYGZus{}handler}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}                     \PYG{c+cm}{/*Call `lv\PYGZus{}task\PYGZus{}handler()` manually to process the wake\PYGZhy{}up event*/}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_get\_inactive\_time()}} you can check \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_count\_running()}} to see if all animations have finished.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Operating system and interrupts}
\label{\detokenize{porting/os:operating-system-and-interrupts}}\label{\detokenize{porting/os::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL is \sphinxstylestrong{not thread\sphinxhyphen{}safe} by default.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, in the following conditions it's valid to call LVGL related functions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxstyleemphasis{events}. Learn more in {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/event::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Events}}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxstyleemphasis{lv\_timer}. Learn more in {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/timer::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Timers}}}}.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Tasks and threads}
\label{\detokenize{porting/os:tasks-and-threads}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you need to use real tasks or threads, you need a mutex which should be invoked before the call of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler}} and released after it.
Also, you have to use the same mutex in other tasks and threads around every LVGL (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_...}}) related function call and code.
This way you can use LVGL in a real multitasking environment. Just make use of a mutex to avoid the concurrent calling of LVGL functions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is some pseudocode to illustrate the concept:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{mutex\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}mutex}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{lvgl\PYGZus{}thread}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
        \PYG{n}{mutex\PYGZus{}lock}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}mutex}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}task\PYGZus{}handler}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{n}{mutex\PYGZus{}unlock}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}mutex}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{n}{thread\PYGZus{}sleep}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{c+cm}{/* sleep for 10 ms */}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{other\PYGZus{}thread}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{c+cm}{/* You must always hold the mutex while using LVGL APIs */}
    \PYG{n}{mutex\PYGZus{}lock}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}mutex}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{img} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}create}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}scr\PYGZus{}act}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{mutex\PYGZus{}unlock}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}mutex}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

    \PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
        \PYG{n}{mutex\PYGZus{}lock}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}mutex}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{c+cm}{/* change to the next image */}
        \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}src}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{img}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{next\PYGZus{}image}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{n}{mutex\PYGZus{}unlock}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{lvgl\PYGZus{}mutex}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{n}{thread\PYGZus{}sleep}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2000}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Interrupts}
\label{\detokenize{porting/os:interrupts}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Try to avoid calling LVGL functions from interrupt handlers (except \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_tick\_inc()}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_flush\_ready()}}). But if you need to do this you have to disable the interrupt which uses LVGL functions while \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler}} is running.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It's a better approach to simply set a flag or some value in the interrupt, and periodically check it in an LVGL timer (which is run by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler}}).

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Logging}
\label{\detokenize{porting/log:logging}}\label{\detokenize{porting/log::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL has a built\sphinxhyphen{}in \sphinxstyleemphasis{Log} module to inform the user about what is happening in the library.


\subsection{Log level}
\label{\detokenize{porting/log:log-level}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To enable logging, set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_USE\_LOG  1}} in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} and set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_LEVEL}} to one of the following values:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_LEVEL\_TRACE}} A lot of logs to give detailed information

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_LEVEL\_INFO}}  Log important events

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_LEVEL\_WARN}}  Log if something unwanted happened but didn't cause a problem

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_LEVEL\_ERROR}} Only critical issues, where the system may fail

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_LEVEL\_USER}} Only user messages

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_LEVEL\_NONE}}  Do not log anything

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The events which have a higher level than the set log level will be logged too. E.g. if you \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_LEVEL\_WARN}}, errors will be also logged.


\subsection{Printing logs}
\label{\detokenize{porting/log:printing-logs}}

\subsubsection{Logging with printf}
\label{\detokenize{porting/log:logging-with-printf}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If your system supports \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{printf}}, you just need to enable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_PRINTF}} in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}} to send the logs with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{printf}}.


\subsubsection{Custom log function}
\label{\detokenize{porting/log:custom-log-function}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you can't use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{printf}} or want to use a custom function to log, you can register a "logger" callback with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_log\_register\_print\_cb()}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{my\PYGZus{}log\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{const} \PYG{k+kt}{char} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{n}{serial\PYGZus{}send}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{strlen}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}


\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}log\PYGZus{}register\PYGZus{}print\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}log\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Add logs}
\label{\detokenize{porting/log:add-logs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also use the log module via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_TRACE/INFO/WARN/ERROR/USER(text)}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG(text)}} functions. Here:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_TRACE/INFO/WARN/ERROR/USER(text)}} append following information to your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{text}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Log Level

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\_\_FILE\_\_

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\_\_LINE\_\_

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\_\_func\_\_

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG(text)}} is similar to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_LOG\_USER}} but has no extra information attached.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Add custom GPU}
\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu:add-custom-gpu}}\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL has a flexible and extendable draw pipeline. You can hook it to do some rendering with a GPU or even completely replace the built\sphinxhyphen{}in software renderer.


\subsection{Draw context}
\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu:draw-context}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The core structure of drawing is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_draw\_ctx\_t}}.
It contains a pointer to a buffer where drawing should happen and a couple of callbacks to draw rectangles, texts, and other primitives.


\subsubsection{Fields}
\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu:fields}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_draw\_ctx\_t}} has the following fields:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void * buf}} Pointer to a buffer to draw into

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_area\_t * buf\_area}} The position and size of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{buf}} (absolute coordinates)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{const lv\_area\_t * clip\_area}} The current clip area with absolute coordinates, always the same or smaller than \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{buf\_area}}. All drawings should be clipped to this area.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*draw\_rect)()}} Draw a rectangle with shadow, gradient, border, etc.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*draw\_arc)()}} Draw an arc

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*draw\_img\_decoded)()}} Draw an (A)RGB image that is already decoded by LVGL.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_res\_t (*draw\_img)()}} Draw an image before decoding it (it bypasses LVGL's internal image decoders)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*draw\_letter)()}} Draw a letter

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*draw\_line)()}} Draw a line

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*draw\_polygon)()}} Draw a polygon

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*draw\_bg)()}} Replace the buffer with a rect without decoration like radius or borders.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*wait\_for\_finish)()}} Wait until all background operation are finished. (E.g. GPU operations)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void * user\_data}} Custom user data for arbitrary purpose

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
(For the sake of simplicity the parameters of the callbacks are not shown here.)

\sphinxAtStartPar
All \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_*}} callbacks receive a pointer to the current \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx}} as their first parameter. Among the other parameters there is a descriptor that tells what to draw,
e.g. for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_rect}} it's called \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/blob/master/src/draw/lv\_draw\_rect.h}{lv\_draw\_rect\_dsc\_t},
for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_draw\_line}} it's called \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/blob/master/src/draw/lv\_draw\_line.h}{lv\_draw\_line\_dsc\_t}, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To correctly render according to a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_dsc}} you need to be familiar with the \sphinxhref{https://docs.lvgl.io/master/overview/coords.html\#boxing-model}{Boxing model} of LVGL and the meanings of the fields. The name and meaning of the fields are identical to name and meaning of the \sphinxhref{https://docs.lvgl.io/master/overview/style-props.html}{Style properties}.


\subsubsection{Initialization}
\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu:initialization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_t}} has 4 fields related to the draw context:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_draw\_ctx\_t * draw\_ctx}} Pointer to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx}} of this display

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*draw\_ctx\_init)(struct \_lv\_disp\_drv\_t * disp\_drv, lv\_draw\_ctx\_t * draw\_ctx)}} Callback to initialize a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*draw\_ctx\_deinit)(struct \_lv\_disp\_drv\_t * disp\_drv, lv\_draw\_ctx\_t * draw\_ctx)}} Callback to de\sphinxhyphen{}initialize a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{size\_t draw\_ctx\_size}} Size of the draw context structure. E.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sizeof(lv\_draw\_sw\_ctx\_t)}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When you ignore these fields, LVGL will set default values for callbacks and size in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_init()}} based on the configuration in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_conf.h}}.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_register()}} will allocate a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx}} based on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx\_size}} and call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx\_init()}} on it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, you can overwrite the callbacks and the size values before calling \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_register()}}.
It makes it possible to use your own \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx}} with your own callbacks.


\subsection{Software renderer}
\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu:software-renderer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL's built in software renderer extends the basic \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_draw\_ctx\_t}} structure and sets the draw callbacks. It looks like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{typedef} \PYG{k}{struct} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
   \PYG{c+cm}{/** Include the basic draw\PYGZus{}ctx type*/}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{base\PYGZus{}draw}\PYG{p}{;}

    \PYG{c+cm}{/** Blend a color or image to an area*/}
    \PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{blend}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{const} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}blend\PYGZus{}dsc\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the draw callbacks in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx\_init()}} like:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{base\PYGZus{}draw}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}rect} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}rect}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{base\PYGZus{}draw}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}letter} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}letter}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Blend callback}
\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu:blend-callback}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As you saw above the software renderer adds the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blend}} callback field. It's a special callback related to how the software renderer works.
All draw operations end up in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blend}} callback which can either fill an area or copy an image to an area by considering an optional mask.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_draw\_sw\_blend\_dsc\_t}} parameter describes what and how to blend. It has the following fields:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{const lv\_area\_t * blend\_area}} The area with absolute coordinates to draw on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx\sphinxhyphen{}>buf}}. If \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src\_buf}} is set, it's the coordinates of the image to blend.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{const lv\_color\_t * src\_buf}} Pointer to an image to blend. If set, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{color}} is ignored. If not set fill \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blend\_area}} with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{color}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_color\_t color}} Fill color. Used only if \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src\_buf == NULL}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_opa\_t * mask\_buf}} NULL if ignored, or an alpha mask to apply on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blend\_area}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_draw\_mask\_res\_t mask\_res}} The result of the previous mask operation. (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_DRAW\_MASK\_RES\_...}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{const lv\_area\_t * mask\_area}} The area of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mask\_buf}} with absolute coordinates

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_opa\_t opa}} The overall opacity

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_blend\_mode\_t blend\_mode}} E.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_BLEND\_MODE\_ADDITIVE}}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Extend the software renderer}
\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu:extend-the-software-renderer}}

\subsubsection{New blend callback}
\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu:new-blend-callback}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let's take a practical example: you would like to use your MCUs GPU for color fill operations only.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As all draw callbacks call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blend}} callback to fill an area in the end only the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blend}} callback needs to be overwritten.

\sphinxAtStartPar
First extend \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_draw\_sw\_ctx\_t}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{c+cm}{/*We don\PYGZsq{}t add new fields, so just for clarity add new type*/}
\PYG{k}{typedef} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Initialize the parent type first */}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}init\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Change some callbacks*/}
    \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{;}

    \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{blend} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}blend}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{base\PYGZus{}draw}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{wait\PYGZus{}for\PYGZus{}finish} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}wait}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After calling \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_draw\_init(\&drv)}} you can assign the new \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx\_init}} callback and set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_ctx\_size}} to overwrite the defaults:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{hor\PYGZus{}res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}hor\PYGZus{}res}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{ver\PYGZus{}res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}ver\PYGZus{}res}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{flush\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}flush\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*New draw ctx settings*/}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}init} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}size} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{k}{sizeof}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}disp\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}register}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This way when LVGL calls \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blend}} it will call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{my\_draw\_blend}} and we can do custom GPU operations. Here is a complete example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}blend}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{const} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}blend\PYGZus{}dsc\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Let\PYGZsq{}s get the blend area which is the intersection of the area to fill and the clip area.*/}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}area\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{blend\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{!}\PYG{n}{\PYGZus{}lv\PYGZus{}area\PYGZus{}intersect}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{blend\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{blend\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{clip\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{k}{return}\PYG{p}{;}  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Fully clipped, nothing to do*/}

    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Fill only non masked, fully opaque, normal blended and not too small areas*/}
    \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{src\PYGZus{}buf} \PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{NULL} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{mask} \PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{NULL} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{opa} \PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}OPA\PYGZus{}MAX} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
       \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{blend\PYGZus{}mode} \PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}BLEND\PYGZus{}MODE\PYGZus{}NORMAL} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}area\PYGZus{}get\PYGZus{}size}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{blend\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}} \PYG{l+m+mi}{100}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}

        \PYG{c+cm}{/*Got the first pixel on the buffer*/}
        \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}coord\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{dest\PYGZus{}stride} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}area\PYGZus{}get\PYGZus{}width}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{c+cm}{/*Width of the destination buffer*/}
        \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}color\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{dest\PYGZus{}buf} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{n}{dest\PYGZus{}buf} \PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{dest\PYGZus{}stride} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{blend\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{y1} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{y1}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{+} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{blend\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{x1} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{x1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

        \PYG{c+cm}{/*Make the blend area relative to the buffer*/}      
        \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}area\PYGZus{}move}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{blend\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{x1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{buf\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{y1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
       
        \PYG{c+cm}{/*Call your custom gou fill function to fill blend\PYGZus{}area, on dest\PYGZus{}buf with dsc\PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{}color*/}  
        \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}fill}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{dest\PYGZus{}buf}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dest\PYGZus{}stride}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{blend\PYGZus{}area}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{color}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Fallback: the GPU doesn\PYGZsq{}t support these settings. Call the SW renderer.*/}
    \PYG{k}{else} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
      \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}blend\PYGZus{}basic}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The implementation of wait callback is much simpler:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{my\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}wait}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}is\PYGZus{}working}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
   
    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Call SW renderer\PYGZsq{}s wait callback too*/}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}wait\PYGZus{}for\PYGZus{}finish}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{New rectangle drawer}
\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu:new-rectangle-drawer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If your MCU has a more powerful GPU that can draw e.g. rounded rectangles you can replace the original software drawer too.
A custom \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{draw\_rect}} callback might look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{my\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}rect}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}ctx\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{const} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}rect\PYGZus{}dsc\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{const} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}area\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{coords}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}mask\PYGZus{}is\PYGZus{}any}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{coords}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{false} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{grad} \PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{NULL} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{bg\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}src} \PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{NULL} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
     \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{shadow\PYGZus{}width} \PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{blend\PYGZus{}mode} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}BLEND\PYGZus{}MODE\PYGZus{}NORMAL}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Draw the background*/}
    \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}bg\PYGZus{}drawer}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{coords}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{bg\PYGZus{}color}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{radius}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
   
    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Draw the border if any*/}
    \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{border\PYGZus{}width}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
      \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}border\PYGZus{}drawer}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{coords}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{border\PYGZus{}width}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{border\PYGZus{}color}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{border\PYGZus{}opa}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
   
    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Draw the outline if any*/}
    \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{outline\PYGZus{}width}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
      \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}outline\PYGZus{}drawer}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{coords}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{outline\PYGZus{}width}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{outline\PYGZus{}color}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{outline\PYGZus{}opa}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{outline\PYGZus{}pad}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
  \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Fallback*/}
  \PYG{k}{else} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}draw\PYGZus{}sw\PYGZus{}rect}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}ctx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{coords}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{my\_draw\_rect}} can fully bypass the use of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blend}} callback if needed.


\subsection{Fully custom draw engine}
\label{\detokenize{porting/gpu:fully-custom-draw-engine}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For example if your MCU/MPU supports a powerful vector graphics engine you might use only that instead of LVGL's SW renderer.
In this case, you need to base the renderer on the basic \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_draw\_ctx\_t}} (instead of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_draw\_sw\_ctx\_t}}) and extend/initialize it as you wish.

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{overview/index:overview}}\label{\detokenize{overview/index::doc}}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{Objects}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:objects}}\label{\detokenize{overview/object::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In LVGL the \sphinxstylestrong{basic building blocks} of a user interface are the objects, also called \sphinxstyleemphasis{Widgets}.
For example a {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/core/btn::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Button}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/core/label::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Label}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/core/img::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Image}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/extra/list::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{List}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/extra/chart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Chart}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/core/textarea::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Text area}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can see all the {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/index::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Object types}}}} here.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All objects are referenced using an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_t}} pointer as a handle. This pointer can later be used to set or get the attributes of the object.


\subsection{Attributes}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:attributes}}

\subsubsection{Basic attributes}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:basic-attributes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All object types share some basic attributes:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Position

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Size

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Parent

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Event handlers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Etc

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can set/get these attributes with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_...}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_get\_...}} functions. For example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set basic object attributes*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}size}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{btn1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{100}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{50}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}	  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set a button\PYGZsq{}s size*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}pos}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{btn1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{20}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mi}{30}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}      \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set a button\PYGZsq{}s position*/}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To see all the available functions visit the {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/obj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Base object's documentation}}}}.


\subsubsection{Specific attributes}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:specific-attributes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The object types have special attributes too. For example, a slider has
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Minimum and maximum values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Current value

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For these special attributes, every object type may have unique API functions. For example for a slider:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set slider specific attributes*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}slider\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}range}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{slider1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{100}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}	   				\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set the min. and max. values*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}slider\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}value}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{slider1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{40}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}ANIM\PYGZus{}ON}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}		\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set the current value (position)*/}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The API of the widgets is described in their {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/index::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Documentation}}}} but you can also check the respective header files (e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{widgets/lv\_slider.h})


\subsection{Working mechanisms}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:working-mechanisms}}

\subsubsection{Parent\sphinxhyphen{}child structure}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:parent-child-structure}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A parent object can be considered as the container of its children. Every object has exactly one parent object (except screens), but a parent can have any number of children.
There is no limitation for the type of the parent but there are objects which are typically a parent (e.g. button) or a child (e.g. label).


\subsubsection{Moving together}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:moving-together}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the position of a parent changes, the children will move along with it.
Therefore, all positions are relative to the parent.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics{{par_child1}.png}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{parent} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}create}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}scr\PYGZus{}act}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}   \PYG{c+cm}{/*Create a parent object on the current screen*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}size}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{parent}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{100}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{80}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}	                 \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set the size of the parent*/}

\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{obj1} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}create}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{parent}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}	         \PYG{c+cm}{/*Create an object on the previously created parent object*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}pos}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{obj1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}	                     \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set the position of the new object*/}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Modify the position of the parent:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics{{par_child2}.png}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}pos}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{parent}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{50}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{50}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}	\PYG{c+cm}{/*Move the parent. The child will move with it.*/}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
(For simplicity the adjusting of colors of the objects is not shown in the example.)


\subsubsection{Visibility only on the parent}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:visibility-only-on-the-parent}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If a child is partially or fully outside its parent then the parts outside will not be visible.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics{{par_child3}.png}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}x}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{obj1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{\PYGZhy{}30}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}	\PYG{c+cm}{/*Move the child a little bit off the parent*/}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This behavior can be overwritten with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_add\_flag(obj, LV\_OBJ\_FLAG\_OVERFLOW\_VISIBLE);}} which allow the children to be drawn out of the parent.


\subsubsection{Create and delete objects}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:create-and-delete-objects}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In LVGL, objects can be created and deleted dynamically at run time. It means only the currently created (existing) objects consume RAM.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This allows for the creation of a screen just when a button is clicked to open it, and for deletion of screens when a new screen is loaded.

\sphinxAtStartPar
UIs can be created based on the current environment of the device. For example one can create meters, charts, bars and sliders based on the currently attached sensors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Every widget has its own \sphinxstylestrong{create} function with a prototype like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{widget}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{\PYGZus{}create}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{parent}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{other} \PYG{n}{parameters} \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{any}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Typically, the create functions only have a \sphinxstyleemphasis{parent} parameter telling them on which object to create the new widget.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The return value is a pointer to the created object with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_t *}} type.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is a common \sphinxstylestrong{delete} function for all object types. It deletes the object and all of its children.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}del}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{obj}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_del}} will delete the object immediately.
If for any reason you can't delete the object immediately you can use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_del\_async(obj)}} which will perform the deletion on the next call of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler()}}.
This is useful e.g. if you want to delete the parent of an object in the child's \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_EVENT\_DELETE}} handler.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can remove all the children of an object (but not the object itself) using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_clean(obj)}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_del\_delayed(obj, 1000)}} to delete an object after some time. The delay is expressed in milliseconds.


\subsection{Screens}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:screens}}

\subsubsection{Create screens}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:create-screens}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The screens are special objects which have no parent object. So they can be created like:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{scr1} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}create}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Screens can be created with any object type. For example, a {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/obj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Base object}}}} or an image to make a wallpaper.


\subsubsection{Get the active screen}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:get-the-active-screen}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There is always an active screen on each display. By default, the library creates and loads a "Base object" as a screen for each display.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To get the currently active screen use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_scr\_act()}} function.


\subsubsection{Load screens}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:load-screens}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To load a new screen, use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_scr\_load(scr1)}}.


\subsubsection{Layers}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:layers}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are two automatically generated layers:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
top layer

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
system layer

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
They are independent of the screens and they will be shown on every screen. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{top layer} is above every object on the screen and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{system layer} is above the \sphinxstyleemphasis{top layer}.
You can add any pop\sphinxhyphen{}up windows to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{top layer} freely. But, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{system layer} is restricted to system\sphinxhyphen{}level things (e.g. mouse cursor will be placed there with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_indev\_set\_cursor()}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_layer\_top()}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_layer\_sys()}} functions return pointers to the top and system layers respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Read the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/layer::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Layer overview}}}} section to learn more about layers.


\paragraph{Load screen with animation}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:load-screen-with-animation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A new screen can be loaded with animation by using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_scr\_load\_anim(scr, transition\_type, time, delay, auto\_del)}}. The following transition types exist:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_SCR\_LOAD\_ANIM\_NONE}} Switch immediately after \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delay}} milliseconds

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_SCR\_LOAD\_ANIM\_OVER\_LEFT/RIGHT/TOP/BOTTOM}} Move the new screen over the current towards the given direction

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_SCR\_LOAD\_ANIM\_OUT\_LEFT/RIGHT/TOP/BOTTOM}} Move out the old screen over the current towards the given direction

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_SCR\_LOAD\_ANIM\_MOVE\_LEFT/RIGHT/TOP/BOTTOM}} Move both the current and new screens towards the given direction

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_SCR\_LOAD\_ANIM\_FADE\_IN/OUT}} Fade the new screen over the old screen, or vice versa

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Setting \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{auto\_del}} to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{true}} will automatically delete the old screen when the animation is finished.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The new screen will become active (returned by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_scr\_act()}}) when the animation starts after \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delay}} time.
All inputs are disabled during the screen animation.


\subsubsection{Handling multiple displays}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:handling-multiple-displays}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Screens are created on the currently selected \sphinxstyleemphasis{default display}.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{default display} is the last registered display with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_drv\_register}}. You can also explicitly select a new default display using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_disp\_set\_default(disp)}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_scr\_act()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_scr\_load()}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_scr\_load\_anim()}} operate on the default display.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Visit {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/display::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Multi\sphinxhyphen{}display support}}}} to learn more.


\subsection{Parts}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:parts}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The widgets are built from multiple parts. For example a {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/obj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Base object}}}} uses the main and scrollbar parts but a {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/core/slider::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Slider}}}} uses the main, indicator and knob parts.
Parts are similar to \sphinxstyleemphasis{pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}elements} in CSS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following predefined parts exist in LVGL:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_PART\_MAIN}} A background like rectangle

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_PART\_SCROLLBAR}}  The scrollbar(s)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_PART\_INDICATOR}} Indicator, e.g. for slider, bar, switch, or the tick box of the checkbox

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_PART\_KNOB}} Like a handle to grab to adjust the value

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_PART\_SELECTED}} Indicate the currently selected option or section

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_PART\_ITEMS}} Used if the widget has multiple similar elements (e.g. table cells)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_PART\_TICKS}} Ticks on scales e.g. for a chart or meter

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_PART\_CURSOR}} Mark a specific place e.g. text area's or chart's cursor

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_PART\_CUSTOM\_FIRST}} Custom parts can be added from here.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The main purpose of parts is to allow styling the "components" of the widgets.
They are described in more detail in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Style overview}}}} section.


\subsection{States}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:states}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The object can be in a combination of the following states:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_DEFAULT}} Normal, released state

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_CHECKED}} Toggled or checked state

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_FOCUSED}} Focused via keypad or encoder or clicked via touchpad/mouse

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_FOCUS\_KEY}} Focused via keypad or encoder but not via touchpad/mouse

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_EDITED}} Edit by an encoder

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_HOVERED}} Hovered by mouse (not supported now)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_PRESSED}} Being pressed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_SCROLLED}} Being scrolled

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_DISABLED}} Disabled state

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_USER\_1}} Custom state

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_USER\_2}} Custom state

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_USER\_3}} Custom state

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_STATE\_USER\_4}} Custom state

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The states are usually automatically changed by the library as the user interacts with an object (presses, releases, focuses, etc.).
However, the states can be changed manually too.
To set or clear given state (but leave the other states untouched) use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_add/clear\_state(obj, LV\_STATE\_...)}}
In both cases OR\sphinxhyphen{}ed state values can be used as well. E.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_add\_state(obj, part, LV\_STATE\_PRESSED | LV\_PRESSED\_CHECKED)}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To learn more about the states read the related section of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Style overview}}}}.


\subsection{Snapshot}
\label{\detokenize{overview/object:snapshot}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A snapshot image can be generated for an object together with its children. Check details in {\hyperref[\detokenize{others/snapshot::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Snapshot}}}}.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Positions, sizes, and layouts}
\label{\detokenize{overview/coords:positions-sizes-and-layouts}}\label{\detokenize{overview/coords::doc}}

\subsection{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{overview/coords:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly to many other parts of LVGL, the concept of setting the coordinates was inspired by CSS. LVGL has by no means a complete implementation of CSS but a comparable subset is implemented (sometimes with minor adjustments).

\sphinxAtStartPar
In short this means:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Explicitly set coordinates are stored in styles (size, position, layouts, etc.)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
support min\sphinxhyphen{}width, max\sphinxhyphen{}width, min\sphinxhyphen{}height, max\sphinxhyphen{}height

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
have pixel, percentage, and "content" units

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
x=0; y=0 coordinate means the top\sphinxhyphen{}left corner of the parent plus the left/top padding plus border width

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
width/height means the full size, the "content area" is smaller with padding and border width

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a subset of flexbox and grid layouts are supported

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Units}
\label{\detokenize{overview/coords:units}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pixel: Simply a position in pixels. An integer always means pixels. E.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_x(btn, 10)}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
percentage: The percentage of the size of the object or its parent (depending on the property). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_pct(value)}} converts a value to percentage. E.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_width(btn, lv\_pct(50))}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_SIZE\_CONTENT}}: Special value to set the width/height of an object to involve all the children. It's similar to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{auto}} in CSS. E.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_width(btn, LV\_SIZE\_CONTENT)}}.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Boxing model}
\label{\detokenize{overview/coords:boxing-model}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL follows CSS's \sphinxhref{https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/box-sizing}{border\sphinxhyphen{}box} model.
An object's "box" is built from the following parts:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bounding box: the width/height of the elements.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
border width: the width of the border.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
padding: space between the sides of the object and its children.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
content: the content area which is the size of the bounding box reduced by the border width and padding.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics{{boxmodel}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The border is drawn inside the bounding box. Inside the border LVGL keeps a "padding margin" when placing an object's children.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The outline is drawn outside the bounding box.


\subsubsection{Important notes}
\label{\detokenize{overview/coords:important-notes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section describes special cases in which LVGL's behavior might be unexpected.


\paragraph{Postponed coordinate calculation}
\label{\detokenize{overview/coords:postponed-coordinate-calculation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL doesn't recalculate all the coordinate changes immediately. This is done to improve performance.
Instead, the objects are marked as "dirty" and before redrawing the screen LVGL checks if there are any "dirty" objects. If so it refreshes their position, size and layout.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In other words, if you need to get the coordinate of an object and the coordinates were just changed, LVGL needs to be forced to recalculate the coordinates.
To do this call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_update\_layout(obj)}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The size and position might depend on the parent or layout. Therefore \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_update\_layout}} recalculates the coordinates of all objects on the screen of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{obj}}.


\paragraph{Removing styles}
\label{\detokenize{overview/coords:removing-styles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As it's described in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/coords:using-styles}]{\emph{Using styles}}} section, coordinates can also be set via style properties.
To be more precise, under the hood every style coordinate related property is stored as a style property. If you use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_x(obj, 20)}} LVGL saves \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{x=20}} in the local style of the object.

\sphinxAtStartPar
