\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_FONT\_UNSCII\_8}} 8 px pixel perfect font with only ASCII characters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_FONT\_UNSCII\_16}} 16 px pixel perfect font with only ASCII characters

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The built\sphinxhyphen{}in fonts are \sphinxstylestrong{global variables} with names like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_font\_montserrat\_16}} for a 16 px height font. To use them in a style, just add a pointer to a font variable like shown above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The built\sphinxhyphen{}in fonts with \sphinxstyleemphasis{bpp = 4} contain the ASCII characters and use the \sphinxhref{https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Montserrat}{Montserrat} font.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to the ASCII range, the following symbols are also added to the built\sphinxhyphen{}in fonts from the \sphinxhref{https://fontawesome.com/}{FontAwesome} font.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics{{symbols}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The symbols can be used singly as:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}label\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}text}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}label}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}SYMBOL\PYGZus{}OK}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Or together with strings (compile time string concatenation):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}label\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}text}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}label}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}SYMBOL\PYGZus{}OK} \PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Apply}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Or more symbols together:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}label\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}text}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}label}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}SYMBOL\PYGZus{}OK} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}SYMBOL\PYGZus{}WIFI} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}SYMBOL\PYGZus{}PLAY}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Special features}
\label{\detokenize{overview/font:special-features}}

\subsubsection{Bidirectional support}
\label{\detokenize{overview/font:bidirectional-support}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Most languages use a Left\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}Right (LTR for short) writing direction, however some languages (such as Hebrew, Persian or Arabic) use Right\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}Left (RTL for short) direction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL not only supports RTL texts but supports mixed (a.k.a. bidirectional, BiDi) text rendering too. Some examples:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics{{bidi}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
BiDi support is enabled by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_USE\_BIDI}} in \sphinxstyleemphasis{lv\_conf.h}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All texts have a base direction (LTR or RTL) which determines some rendering rules and the default alignment of the text (Left or Right).
However, in LVGL, the base direction is not only applied to labels. It's a general property which can be set for every object.
If not set then it will be inherited from the parent.
This means it's enough to set the base direction of a screen and every object will inherit it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default base direction for screens can be set by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_BIDI\_BASE\_DIR\_DEF}} in \sphinxstyleemphasis{lv\_conf.h} and other objects inherit the base direction from their parent.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To set an object's base direction use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_style\_base\_dir(obj, base\_dir,selector)}}.  The possible base directions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_BASE\_DIR\_LTR}}: Left to Right base direction

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_BASE\_DIR\_RTL}}: Right to Left base direction

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_BASE\_DIR\_AUTO}}: Auto detect base direction

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_BASE\_DIR\_NEUTRAL}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_BASE\_DIR\_WEAK}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This list summarizes the effect of RTL base direction on objects:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Create objects by default on the right

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_tabview}}: Displays tabs from right to left

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_checkbox}}: Shows the box on the right

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_btnmatrix}}: Shows buttons from right to left

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_list}}: Shows icons on the right

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_dropdown}}: Aligns options to the right

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_bar}}: Shows progress from right to left

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The texts in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_table}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_btnmatrix}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_keyboard}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_tabview}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_dropdown}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_roller}} are "BiDi processed" to be displayed correctly

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Arabic and Persian support}
\label{\detokenize{overview/font:arabic-and-persian-support}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are some special rules to display Arabic and Persian characters: the \sphinxstyleemphasis{form} of a character depends on its position in the text.
A different form of the same letter needs to be used when it is isolated, at start, middle or end positions. Besides these, some conjunction rules should also be taken into account.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL supports these rules if \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_USE\_ARABIC\_PERSIAN\_CHARS}} is enabled.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, there are some limitations:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Only displaying text is supported (e.g. on labels), text inputs (e.g. text area) don't support this feature.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Static text (i.e. const) is not processed. E.g. texts set by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_label\_set\_text()}} will be "Arabic processed" but \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_lable\_set\_text\_static()}} won't.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Text get functions (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_label\_get\_text()}}) will return the processed text.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Subpixel rendering}
\label{\detokenize{overview/font:subpixel-rendering}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Subpixel rendering allows for tripling the horizontal resolution by rendering anti\sphinxhyphen{}aliased edges on Red, Green and Blue channels instead of at pixel level granularity. This takes advantage of the position of physical color channels of each pixel, resulting in higher quality letter anti\sphinxhyphen{}aliasing. Learn more \sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subpixel\_rendering}{here}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For subpixel rendering, the fonts need to be generated with special settings:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the online converter tick the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Subpixel}} box

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the command line tool use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}lcd}} flag. Note that the generated font needs about three times more memory.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Subpixel rendering works only if the color channels of the pixels have a horizontal layout. That is the R, G, B channels are next to each other and not above each other.
The order of color channels also needs to match with the library settings. By default, LVGL assumes \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RGB}} order, however this can be swapped by setting \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_SUBPX\_BGR  1}} in \sphinxstyleemphasis{lv\_conf.h}.


\subsubsection{Compressed fonts}
\label{\detokenize{overview/font:compressed-fonts}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The bitmaps of fonts can be compressed by
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ticking the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Compressed}} check box in the online converter

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
not passing the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}no\sphinxhyphen{}compress}} flag to the offline converter (compression is applied by default)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compression is more effective with larger fonts and higher bpp. However, it's about 30\% slower to render compressed fonts.
Therefore, it's recommended to compress only the largest fonts of a user interface, because
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
they need the most memory

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
they can be compressed better

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
and probably they are used less frequently then the medium\sphinxhyphen{}sized fonts, so the performance cost is smaller.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Add a new font}
\label{\detokenize{overview/font:add-a-new-font}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are several ways to add a new font to your project:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest method is to use the \sphinxhref{https://lvgl.io/tools/fontconverter}{Online font converter}. Just set the parameters, click the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Convert} button, copy the font to your project and use it. \sphinxstylestrong{Be sure to carefully read the steps provided on that site or you will get an error while converting.}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lv\_font\_conv}{Offline font converter}. (Requires Node.js to be installed)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to create something like the built\sphinxhyphen{}in fonts (Montserrat font and symbols) but in a different size and/or ranges, you can use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{built\_in\_font\_gen.py}} script in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lvgl/scripts/built\_in\_font}} folder.
(This requires Python and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_font\_conv}} to be installed)

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To declare a font in a file, use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_FONT\_DECLARE(my\_font\_name)}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To make fonts globally available (like the built\sphinxhyphen{}in fonts), add them to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_FONT\_CUSTOM\_DECLARE}} in \sphinxstyleemphasis{lv\_conf.h}.


\subsection{Add new symbols}
\label{\detokenize{overview/font:add-new-symbols}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The built\sphinxhyphen{}in symbols are created from the \sphinxhref{https://fontawesome.com/}{FontAwesome} font.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Search for a symbol on \sphinxurl{https://fontawesome.com}. For example the \sphinxhref{https://fontawesome.com/icons/usb?style=brands}{USB symbol}. Copy its Unicode ID which is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0xf287}} in this case.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open the \sphinxhref{https://lvgl.io/tools/fontconverter}{Online font converter}. Add \sphinxhref{https://lvgl.io/assets/others/FontAwesome5-Solid+Brands+Regular.woff}{FontAwesome.woff}. .

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the parameters such as Name, Size, BPP. You'll use this name to declare and use the font in your code.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add the Unicode ID of the symbol to the range field. E.g.\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ 0xf287}} for the USB symbol. More symbols can be enumerated with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{,}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Convert the font and copy the generated source code to your project. Make sure to compile the .c file of your font.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Declare the font using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{extern lv\_font\_t my\_font\_name;}} or simply use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_FONT\_DECLARE(my\_font\_name);}}.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Using the symbol}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Convert the Unicode value to UTF8, for example on \sphinxhref{http://www.ltg.ed.ac.uk/~richard/utf-8.cgi?input=f287\&mode=hex}{this site}. For \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0xf287}} the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Hex UTF\sphinxhyphen{}8 bytes} are \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{EF 8A 87}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Create a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{define}} string from the UTF8 values: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#define MY\_USB\_SYMBOL "\textbackslash{}xEF\textbackslash{}x8A\textbackslash{}x87"}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Create a label and set the text. Eg. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_label\_set\_text(label, MY\_USB\_SYMBOL)}}

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note \sphinxhyphen{} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_label\_set\_text(label, MY\_USB\_SYMBOL)}} searches for this symbol in the font defined in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{style.text.font}} properties. To use the symbol you may need to change it. Eg \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ style.text.font = my\_font\_name}}


\subsection{Load a font at run\sphinxhyphen{}time}
\label{\detokenize{overview/font:load-a-font-at-run-time}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_font\_load}} can be used to load a font from a file. The font needs to have a special binary format. (Not TTF or WOFF).
Use \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lv\_font\_conv/}{lv\_font\_conv} with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}format bin}} option to generate an LVGL compatible font file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that to load a font {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/file-system::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{LVGL's filesystem}}}} needs to be enabled and a driver must be added.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}load}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{X}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{path}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{to}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{bin}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Use the font*/}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Free the font if not required anymore*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}free}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Add a new font engine}
\label{\detokenize{overview/font:add-a-new-font-engine}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL's font interface is designed to be very flexible but, even so, you can add your own font engine in place of LVGL's internal one.
For example, you can use \sphinxhref{https://www.freetype.org/}{FreeType} to real\sphinxhyphen{}time render glyphs from TTF fonts or use an external flash to store the font's bitmap and read them when the library needs them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A ready to use FreeType can be found in \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lv\_lib\_freetype}{lv\_freetype} repository.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To do this, a custom \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_font\_t}} variable needs to be created:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/*Describe the properties of a font*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}glyph\PYGZus{}dsc} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}get\PYGZus{}glyph\PYGZus{}dsc\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}        \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set a callback to get info about glyphs*/}
\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}glyph\PYGZus{}bitmap} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}get\PYGZus{}glyph\PYGZus{}bitmap\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set a callback to get bitmap of a glyph*/}
\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{line\PYGZus{}height} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{height}\PYG{p}{;}                       \PYG{c+cm}{/*The real line height where any text fits*/}
\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{base\PYGZus{}line} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{base\PYGZus{}line}\PYG{p}{;}                      \PYG{c+cm}{/*Base line measured from the top of line\PYGZus{}height*/}
\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{dsc} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{something\PYGZus{}required}\PYG{p}{;}                   \PYG{c+cm}{/*Store any implementation specific data here*/}
\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{user\PYGZus{}data} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{user\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{p}{;}                      \PYG{c+cm}{/*Optionally some extra user data*/}

\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}

\PYG{c+cm}{/* Get info about glyph of `unicode\PYGZus{}letter` in `font` font.}
\PYG{c+cm}{ * Store the result in `dsc\PYGZus{}out`.}
\PYG{c+cm}{ * The next letter (`unicode\PYGZus{}letter\PYGZus{}next`) might be used to calculate the width required by this glyph (kerning)}
\PYG{c+cm}{ */}
\PYG{k+kt}{bool} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}get\PYGZus{}glyph\PYGZus{}dsc\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{const} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{font}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}glyph\PYGZus{}dsc\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{dsc\PYGZus{}out}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k+kt}{uint32\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{unicode\PYGZus{}letter}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k+kt}{uint32\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{unicode\PYGZus{}letter\PYGZus{}next}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Your code here*/}

    \PYG{c+cm}{/* Store the result.}
\PYG{c+cm}{     * For example ...}
\PYG{c+cm}{     */}
    \PYG{n}{dsc\PYGZus{}out}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{adv\PYGZus{}w} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{12}\PYG{p}{;}        \PYG{c+cm}{/*Horizontal space required by the glyph in [px]*/}
    \PYG{n}{dsc\PYGZus{}out}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{box\PYGZus{}h} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{8}\PYG{p}{;}         \PYG{c+cm}{/*Height of the bitmap in [px]*/}
    \PYG{n}{dsc\PYGZus{}out}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{box\PYGZus{}w} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{6}\PYG{p}{;}         \PYG{c+cm}{/*Width of the bitmap in [px]*/}
    \PYG{n}{dsc\PYGZus{}out}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{ofs\PYGZus{}x} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}         \PYG{c+cm}{/*X offset of the bitmap in [pf]*/}
    \PYG{n}{dsc\PYGZus{}out}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{ofs\PYGZus{}y} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{;}         \PYG{c+cm}{/*Y offset of the bitmap measured from the as line*/}
    \PYG{n}{dsc\PYGZus{}out}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{bpp}   \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{;}         \PYG{c+cm}{/*Bits per pixel: 1/2/4/8*/}

    \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{p}{;}                \PYG{c+cm}{/*true: glyph found; false: glyph was not found*/}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}


\PYG{c+cm}{/* Get the bitmap of `unicode\PYGZus{}letter` from `font`. */}
\PYG{k}{const} \PYG{k+kt}{uint8\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}get\PYGZus{}glyph\PYGZus{}bitmap\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{const} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{font}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k+kt}{uint32\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{unicode\PYGZus{}letter}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{c+cm}{/* Your code here */}

    \PYG{c+cm}{/* The bitmap should be a continuous bitstream where}
\PYG{c+cm}{     * each pixel is represented by `bpp` bits */}

    \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{n}{bitmap}\PYG{p}{;}    \PYG{c+cm}{/*Or NULL if not found*/}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Use font fallback}
\label{\detokenize{overview/font:use-font-fallback}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fallback}} in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_font\_t}} to provide fallback to the font. When the font
fails to find glyph to a letter, it will try to let font from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fallback}} to handle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fallback}} can be chained, so it will try to solve until there is no \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fallback}} set.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/* Roboto font doesn\PYGZsq{}t have support for CJK glyphs */}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{roboto} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}load\PYGZus{}function}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{c+cm}{/* Droid Sans Fallback has more glyphs but its typeface doesn\PYGZsq{}t look good as Roboto */}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{droid\PYGZus{}sans\PYGZus{}fallback} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}font\PYGZus{}load\PYGZus{}function}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{c+cm}{/* So now we can display Roboto for supported characters while having wider characters set support */}
\PYG{n}{roboto}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{fallback} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{droid\PYGZus{}sans\PYGZus{}fallback}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Images}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:images}}\label{\detokenize{overview/image::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
An image can be a file or a variable which stores the bitmap itself and some metadata.


\subsection{Store images}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:store-images}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can store images in two places
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
as a variable in internal memory (RAM or ROM)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
as a file

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Variables}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:variables}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Images stored internally in a variable are composed mainly of an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_img\_dsc\_t}} structure with the following fields:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{header}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cf} Color format. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/image:color-format}]{\emph{below}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{w} width in pixels (<= 2048)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{h} height in pixels (<= 2048)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{always zero} 3 bits which need to be always zero

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{reserved} reserved for future use

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{data} pointer to an array where the image itself is stored

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{data\_size} length of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data}} in bytes

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are usually stored within a project as C files. They are linked into the resulting executable like any other constant data.


\subsubsection{Files}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:files}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To deal with files you need to add a storage \sphinxstyleemphasis{Drive} to LVGL. In short, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Drive} is a collection of functions (\sphinxstyleemphasis{open}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{read}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{close}, etc.) registered in LVGL to make file operations.
You can add an interface to a standard file system (FAT32 on SD card) or you create your simple file system to read data from an SPI Flash memory.
In every case, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Drive} is just an abstraction to read and/or write data to memory.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/file-system::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{File system}}}} section to learn more.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Images stored as files are not linked into the resulting executable, and must be read into RAM before being drawn. As a result, they are not as resource\sphinxhyphen{}friendly as images linked at compile time. However, they are easier to replace without needing to rebuild the main program.


\subsection{Color formats}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:color-formats}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Various built\sphinxhyphen{}in color formats are supported:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR} Simply stores the RGB colors (in whatever color depth LVGL is configured for).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR\_ALPHA} Like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR}} but it also adds an alpha (transparency) byte for every pixel.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR\_CHROMA\_KEYED} Like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR}} but if a pixel has the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_COLOR\_TRANSP}} color (set in \sphinxstyleemphasis{lv\_conf.h}) it will be transparent.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{LV\_IMG\_CF\_INDEXED\_1/2/4/8BIT} Uses a palette with 2, 4, 16 or 256 colors and stores each pixel in 1, 2, 4 or 8 bits.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{LV\_IMG\_CF\_ALPHA\_1/2/4/8BIT} \sphinxstylestrong{Only stores the Alpha value with 1, 2, 4 or 8 bits.} The pixels take the color of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{style.img\_recolor}} and the set opacity. The source image has to be an alpha channel. This is ideal for bitmaps similar to fonts where the whole image is one color that can be altered.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The bytes of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR}} images are stored in the following order.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For 32\sphinxhyphen{}bit color depth:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Byte 0: Blue

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Byte 1: Green

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Byte 2: Red

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Byte 3: Alpha

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For 16\sphinxhyphen{}bit color depth:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Byte 0: Green 3 lower bit, Blue 5 bit

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Byte 1: Red 5 bit, Green 3 higher bit

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Byte 2: Alpha byte (only with LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR\_ALPHA)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For 8\sphinxhyphen{}bit color depth:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Byte 0: Red 3 bit, Green 3 bit, Blue 2 bit

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Byte 2: Alpha byte (only with LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR\_ALPHA)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can store images in a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Raw} format to indicate that it's not encoded with one of the built\sphinxhyphen{}in color formats and an external {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/image:image-decoder}]{\emph{Image decoder}}} needs to be used to decode the image.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{LV\_IMG\_CF\_RAW} Indicates a basic raw image (e.g. a PNG or JPG image).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{LV\_IMG\_CF\_RAW\_ALPHA} Indicates that an image has alpha and an alpha byte is added for every pixel.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{LV\_IMG\_CF\_RAW\_CHROMA\_KEYED} Indicates that an image is chroma\sphinxhyphen{}keyed as described in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR\_CHROMA\_KEYED}} above.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Add and use images}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:add-and-use-images}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can add images to LVGL in two ways:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
using the online converter

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
manually create images

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Online converter}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:online-converter}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The online Image converter is available here: https://lvgl.io/tools/imageconverter

\sphinxAtStartPar
Adding an image to LVGL via the online converter is easy.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
You need to select a \sphinxstyleemphasis{BMP}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{PNG} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{JPG} image first.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Give the image a name that will be used within LVGL.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Select the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/image:color-formats}]{\emph{Color format}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Select the type of image you want. Choosing a binary will generate a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.bin}} file that must be stored separately and read using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/image:files}]{\emph{file support}}}. Choosing a variable will generate a standard C file that can be linked into your project.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Hit the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Convert} button. Once the conversion is finished, your browser will automatically download the resulting file.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the generated C arrays (variables), bitmaps for all the color depths (1, 8, 16 or 32) are included in the C file, but only the color depth that matches \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_COLOR\_DEPTH}} in \sphinxstyleemphasis{lv\_conf.h} will actually be linked into the resulting executable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the case of binary files, you need to specify the color format you want:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
RGB332 for 8\sphinxhyphen{}bit color depth

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
RGB565 for 16\sphinxhyphen{}bit color depth

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
RGB565 Swap for 16\sphinxhyphen{}bit color depth (two bytes are swapped)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
RGB888 for 32\sphinxhyphen{}bit color depth

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Manually create an image}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:manually-create-an-image}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are generating an image at run\sphinxhyphen{}time, you can craft an image variable to display it using LVGL. For example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{uint8\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mh}{0x00}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mh}{0x01}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mh}{0x02}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}dsc\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}dsc} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{header}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{always\PYGZus{}zero} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{header}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{w} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{80}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{header}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{h} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{60}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{data\PYGZus{}size} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{80} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{l+m+mi}{60} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}COLOR\PYGZus{}DEPTH} \PYG{o}{/} \PYG{l+m+mi}{8}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{header}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{cf} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}IMG\PYGZus{}CF\PYGZus{}TRUE\PYGZus{}COLOR}\PYG{p}{,}          \PYG{c+cm}{/*Set the color format*/}
    \PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{data} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the color format is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR\_ALPHA}} you can set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data\_size}} like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{80 * 60 * LV\_IMG\_PX\_SIZE\_ALPHA\_BYTE}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another (possibly simpler) option to create and display an image at run\sphinxhyphen{}time is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/core/canvas::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Canvas}}}} object.


\subsubsection{Use images}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:use-images}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to use an image in LVGL is to display it with an {\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/core/img::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{lv\_img}}}} object:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{icon} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}create}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}scr\PYGZus{}act}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*From variable*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}src}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{icon}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}icon\PYGZus{}dsc}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*From file*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}src}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{icon}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{S:my\PYGZus{}icon.bin}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the image was converted with the online converter, you should use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_DECLARE(my\_icon\_dsc)}} to declare the image in the file where you want to use it.


\subsection{Image decoder}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:image-decoder}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As you can see in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/image:color-formats}]{\emph{Color formats}}} section, LVGL supports several built\sphinxhyphen{}in image formats. In many cases, these will be all you need. LVGL doesn't directly support, however, generic image formats like PNG or JPG.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To handle non\sphinxhyphen{}built\sphinxhyphen{}in image formats, you need to use external libraries and attach them to LVGL via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Image decoder} interface.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An image decoder consists of 4 callbacks:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{info} get some basic info about the image (width, height and color format).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{open} open an image: either store a decoded image or set it to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} to indicate the image can be read line\sphinxhyphen{}by\sphinxhyphen{}line.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{read} if \sphinxstyleemphasis{open} didn't fully open an image this function should give some decoded data (max 1 line) from a given position.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{close} close an opened image, free the allocated resources.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can add any number of image decoders. When an image needs to be drawn, the library will try all the registered image decoders until it finds one which can open the image, i.e. one which knows that format.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_TRUE\_COLOR\_...}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_INDEXED\_...}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_ALPHA\_...}} formats (essentially, all non\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RAW}} formats) are understood by the built\sphinxhyphen{}in decoder.


\subsubsection{Custom image formats}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:custom-image-formats}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The easiest way to create a custom image is to use the online image converter and select \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Raw}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Raw with alpha}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Raw with chroma\sphinxhyphen{}keyed}} format. It will just take every byte of the binary file you uploaded and write it as an image "bitmap". You then need to attach an image decoder that will parse that bitmap and generate the real, renderable bitmap.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{header.cf}} will be \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_RAW}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_RAW\_ALPHA}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_RAW\_CHROMA\_KEYED}} accordingly. You should choose the correct format according to your needs: a fully opaque image, using an alpha channel or using a chroma key.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After decoding, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{raw} formats are considered \sphinxstyleemphasis{True color} by the library. In other words, the image decoder must decode the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Raw} images to \sphinxstyleemphasis{True color} according to the format described in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/image:color-formats}]{\emph{Color formats}}} section.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to create a custom image, you should use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_USER\_ENCODED\_0..7}} color formats. However, the library can draw images only in \sphinxstyleemphasis{True color} format (or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Raw} but ultimately it will be in \sphinxstyleemphasis{True color} format).
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_USER\_ENCODED\_...}} formats are not known by the library and therefore they should be decoded to one of the known formats from the {\hyperref[\detokenize{overview/image:color-formats}]{\emph{Color formats}}} section.
It's possible to decode an image to a non\sphinxhyphen{}true color format first (for example: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_INDEXED\_4BITS}}) and then call the built\sphinxhyphen{}in decoder functions to convert it to \sphinxstyleemphasis{True color}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With \sphinxstyleemphasis{User encoded} formats, the color format in the open function (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dsc\sphinxhyphen{}>header.cf}}) should be changed according to the new format.


\subsubsection{Register an image decoder}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:register-an-image-decoder}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here's an example of getting LVGL to work with PNG images.

\sphinxAtStartPar
First, you need to create a new image decoder and set some functions to open/close the PNG files. It should look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/*Create a new decoder and register functions */}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoder\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{dec} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoder\PYGZus{}create}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoder\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}info\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{dec}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{decoder\PYGZus{}info}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

  \PYG{n}{header}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{w} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{width}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{ */}
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}res\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n+nf}{decoder\PYGZus{}open}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoder\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{decoder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoder\PYGZus{}dsc\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+cm}{ */}
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{decoder\PYGZus{}close}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoder\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{decoder}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoder\PYGZus{}dsc\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{p}{)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
So in summary:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decoder\_info}}, you should collect some basic information about the image and store it in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{header}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decoder\_open}}, you should try to open the image source pointed by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dsc\sphinxhyphen{}>src}}. Its type is already in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dsc\sphinxhyphen{}>src\_type == LV\_IMG\_SRC\_FILE/VARIABLE}}.
If this format/type is not supported by the decoder, return \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_RES\_INV}}.
However, if you can open the image, a pointer to the decoded \sphinxstyleemphasis{True color} image should be set in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dsc\sphinxhyphen{}>img\_data}}.
If the format is known, but you don't want to decode the entire image (e.g. no memory for it), set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dsc\sphinxhyphen{}>img\_data = NULL}} and use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{read\_line}} to get the pixel data.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decoder\_close}} you should free all allocated resources.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decoder\_read}} is optional. Decoding the whole image requires extra memory and some computational overhead.
However, it can decode one line of the image without decoding the whole image, you can save memory and time.
To indicate that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{line read} function should be used, set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dsc\sphinxhyphen{}>img\_data = NULL}} in the open function.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Manually use an image decoder}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:manually-use-an-image-decoder}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL will use registered image decoders automatically if you try and draw a raw image (i.e. using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_img}} object) but you can use them manually too. Create an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_img\_decoder\_dsc\_t}} variable to describe the decoding session and call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_img\_decoder\_open()}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{color}} parameter is used only with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CF\_ALPHA\_1/2/4/8BIT}} images to tell color of the image.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{frame\_id}} can be used if the image to open is an animation.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}res\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{res}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoder\PYGZus{}dsc\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoder\PYGZus{}open}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}dsc}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{color}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{frame\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{res} \PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}RES\PYGZus{}OK}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Do something with `dsc\PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{}img\PYGZus{}data`*/}
  \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}img\PYGZus{}decoder\PYGZus{}close}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{dsc}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Image caching}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:image-caching}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sometimes it takes a lot of time to open an image.
Continuously decoding a PNG image or loading images from a slow external memory would be inefficient and detrimental to the user experience.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Therefore, LVGL caches a given number of images. Caching means some images will be left open, hence LVGL can quickly access them from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dsc\sphinxhyphen{}>img\_data}} instead of needing to decode them again.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Of course, caching images is resource intensive as it uses more RAM to store the decoded image. LVGL tries to optimize the process as much as possible (see below), but you will still need to evaluate if this would be beneficial for your platform or not. Image caching may not be worth it if you have a deeply embedded target which decodes small images from a relatively fast storage medium.


\subsubsection{Cache size}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:cache-size}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of cache entries can be defined with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_IMG\_CACHE\_DEF\_SIZE}} in \sphinxstyleemphasis{lv\_conf.h}. The default value is 1 so only the most recently used image will be left open.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The size of the cache can be changed at run\sphinxhyphen{}time with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_img\_cache\_set\_size(entry\_num)}}.


\subsubsection{Value of images}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:value-of-images}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When you use more images than cache entries, LVGL can't cache all the images. Instead, the library will close one of the cached images to free space.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To decide which image to close, LVGL uses a measurement it previously made of how long it took to open the image. Cache entries that hold slower\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}open images are considered more valuable and are kept in the cache as long as possible.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want or need to override LVGL's measurement, you can manually set the \sphinxstyleemphasis{time to open} value in the decoder open function in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dsc\sphinxhyphen{}>time\_to\_open = time\_ms}} to give a higher or lower value. (Leave it unchanged to let LVGL control it.)

\sphinxAtStartPar
Every cache entry has a \sphinxstyleemphasis{"life"} value. Every time an image is opened through the cache, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{life} value of all entries is decreased to make them older.
When a cached image is used, its \sphinxstyleemphasis{life} value is increased by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{time to open} value to make it more alive.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If there is no more space in the cache, the entry with the lowest life value will be closed.


\subsubsection{Memory usage}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:memory-usage}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that a cached image might continuously consume memory. For example, if three PNG images are cached, they will consume memory while they are open.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Therefore, it's the user's responsibility to be sure there is enough RAM to cache even the largest images at the same time.


\subsubsection{Clean the cache}
\label{\detokenize{overview/image:clean-the-cache}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let's say you have loaded a PNG image into a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_img\_dsc\_t my\_png}} variable and use it in an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_img}} object. If the image is already cached and you then change the underlying PNG file, you need to notify LVGL to cache the image again. Otherwise, there is no easy way of detecting that the underlying file changed and LVGL will still draw the old image from cache.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To do this, use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_img\_cache\_invalidate\_src(\&my\_png)}}. If \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} is passed as a parameter, the whole cache will be cleaned.

\section{File system}
\label{\detokenize{overview/file-system:file-system}}\label{\detokenize{overview/file-system::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL has a 'File system' abstraction module that enables you to attach any type of file system.
A file system is identified by an assigned drive letter.
For example, if an SD card is associated with the letter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{'S'}}, a file can be reached using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"S:path/to/file.txt"}}.


\subsection{Ready to use drivers}
\label{\detokenize{overview/file-system:ready-to-use-drivers}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lv\_fs\_if}{lv\_fs\_if} repository contains prepared drivers using POSIX, standard C and the \sphinxhref{http://elm-chan.org/fsw/ff/00index\_e.html}{FATFS} API.
See its \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lv\_fs\_if\#readme}{README} for the details.


\subsection{Adding a driver}
\label{\detokenize{overview/file-system:adding-a-driver}}

\subsubsection{Registering a driver}
\label{\detokenize{overview/file-system:registering-a-driver}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To add a driver, a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_fs\_drv\_t}} needs to be initialized like below. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_fs\_drv\_t}} needs to be static, global or dynamically allocated and not a local variable.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{;}                   \PYG{c+cm}{/*Needs to be static or global*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}                     \PYG{c+cm}{/*Basic initialization*/}

\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{letter} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+sc}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+sc}{S}\PYG{l+s+sc}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{;}                         \PYG{c+cm}{/*An uppercase letter to identify the drive */}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{cache\PYGZus{}size} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}cache\PYGZus{}size}\PYG{p}{;}           \PYG{c+cm}{/*Cache size for reading in bytes. 0 to not cache.*/}

\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{ready\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}ready\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}               \PYG{c+cm}{/*Callback to tell if the drive is ready to use */}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{open\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}open\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}                 \PYG{c+cm}{/*Callback to open a file */}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{close\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}close\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}               \PYG{c+cm}{/*Callback to close a file */}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}read\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}                 \PYG{c+cm}{/*Callback to read a file */}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{write\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}write\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}               \PYG{c+cm}{/*Callback to write a file */}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{seek\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}seek\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}                 \PYG{c+cm}{/*Callback to seek in a file (Move cursor) */}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{tell\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}tell\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}                 \PYG{c+cm}{/*Callback to tell the cursor position  */}

\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{dir\PYGZus{}open\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}dir\PYGZus{}open\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}         \PYG{c+cm}{/*Callback to open directory to read its content */}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{dir\PYGZus{}read\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}dir\PYGZus{}read\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}         \PYG{c+cm}{/*Callback to read a directory\PYGZsq{}s content */}
\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{dir\PYGZus{}close\PYGZus{}cb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}dir\PYGZus{}close\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{;}       \PYG{c+cm}{/*Callback to close a directory */}

\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{user\PYGZus{}data} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}user\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{p}{;}             \PYG{c+cm}{/*Any custom data if required*/}

\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}register}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}                 \PYG{c+cm}{/*Finally register the drive*/}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Any of the callbacks can be \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} to indicate that operation is not supported.


\subsubsection{Implementing the callbacks}
\label{\detokenize{overview/file-system:implementing-the-callbacks}}

\paragraph{Open callback}
\label{\detokenize{overview/file-system:open-callback}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The prototype of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{open\_cb}} looks like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{open\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{const} \PYG{k+kt}{char} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{path}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}mode\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{path}} is the path after the drive letter (e.g. "S:path/to/file.txt" \sphinxhyphen{}> "path/to/file.txt"). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mode}} can be \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_FS\_MODE\_WR}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_FS\_MODE\_RD}} to open for writes or reads.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The return value is a pointer to a \sphinxstyleemphasis{file object} that describes the opened file or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} if there were any issues (e.g. the file wasn't found).
The returned file object will be passed to other file system related callbacks. (see below)


\subsubsection{Other callbacks}
\label{\detokenize{overview/file-system:other-callbacks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The other callbacks are quite similar. For example \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{write\_cb}} looks like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}res\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{write\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}drv\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{drv}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{file\PYGZus{}p}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k}{const} \PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k+kt}{uint32\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{btw}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{k+kt}{uint32\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{bw}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{file\_p}}, LVGL passes the return value of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{open\_cb}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{buf}} is the data to write, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{btw}} is the Bytes To Write, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bw}} is the actually written bytes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a template of these callbacks see \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl/blob/master/examples/porting/lv\_port\_fs\_template.c}{lv\_fs\_template.c}.


\subsection{Usage example}
\label{\detokenize{overview/file-system:usage-example}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The example below shows how to read from a file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}file\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}res\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{res}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}open}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{S:folder/file.txt}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}FS\PYGZus{}MODE\PYGZus{}RD}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{res} \PYG{o}{!}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}FS\PYGZus{}RES\PYGZus{}OK}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}error\PYGZus{}handling}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k+kt}{uint32\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}num}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{uint8\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{8}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{8}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}num}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{res} \PYG{o}{!}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}FS\PYGZus{}RES\PYGZus{}OK} \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|} \PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}num} \PYG{o}{!}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{8}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}error\PYGZus{}handling}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}close}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{The mode in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_fs\_open}} can be \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_FS\_MODE\_WR}} to open for writes only or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LV\_FS\_MODE\_RD | LV\_FS\_MODE\_WR}} for both}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This example shows how to read a directory's content. It's up to the driver how to mark directories in the result but it can be a good practice to insert a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{'/'}} in front of each directory name.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}dir\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{dir}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}res\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{res}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}dir\PYGZus{}open}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{dir}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{S:/folder}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{res} \PYG{o}{!}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}FS\PYGZus{}RES\PYGZus{}OK}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}error\PYGZus{}handling}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k+kt}{char} \PYG{n}{fn}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{256}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{n}{res} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}fs\PYGZus{}dir\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{dir}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{fn}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{res} \PYG{o}{!}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{LV\PYGZus{}FS\PYGZus{}RES\PYGZus{}OK}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
        \PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}error\PYGZus{}handling}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
        \PYG{k}{break}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

    \PYG{c+cm}{/*fn is empty, if not more files to read*/}

{\hyperref[\detokenize{widgets/core/img::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Image}}}} objects can be opened from files too (besides variables stored in the compiled program).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
read

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
seek

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
tell

\end{itemize}

\section{Animations}
\label{\detokenize{overview/animation:animations}}\label{\detokenize{overview/animation::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can automatically change the value of a variable between a start and an end value using animations.
Animation will happen by periodically calling an "animator" function with the corresponding value parameter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{animator} functions have the following prototype:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{func}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{var}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}var\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{value}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This prototype is compatible with the majority of the property \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} functions in LVGL. For example \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_x(obj, value)}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_width(obj, value)}}


\subsection{Create an animation}
\label{\detokenize{overview/animation:create-an-animation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To create an animation an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_t}} variable has to be initialized and configured with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_set\_...()}} functions.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{c+cm}{/* INITIALIZE AN ANIMATION}
\PYG{c+cm}{ *\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}*/}

\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/* MANDATORY SETTINGS}
\PYG{c+cm}{ *\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}*/}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set the \PYGZdq{}animator\PYGZdq{} function*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}exec\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}exec\PYGZus{}xcb\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}x}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set target of the animation*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}var}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{obj}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Length of the animation [ms]*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}time}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{duration}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set start and end values. E.g. 0, 150*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}values}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{start}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{end}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/* OPTIONAL SETTINGS}
\PYG{c+cm}{ *\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}*/}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Time to wait before starting the animation [ms]*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}delay}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{delay}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set path (curve). Default is linear*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}path\PYGZus{}ease\PYGZus{}in}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set a callback to indicate when the animation is ready (idle).*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}ready\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{ready\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set a callback to indicate when the animation is deleted (idle).*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}deleted\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{deleted\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Set a callback to indicate when the animation is started (after delay).*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}start\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{start\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*When ready, play the animation backward with this duration. Default is 0 (disabled) [ms]*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}playback\PYGZus{}time}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{time}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Delay before playback. Default is 0 (disabled) [ms]*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}playback\PYGZus{}delay}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{delay}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Number of repetitions. Default is 1. LV\PYGZus{}ANIM\PYGZus{}REPEAT\PYGZus{}INFINITE for infinite repetition*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}repeat\PYGZus{}count}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{cnt}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Delay before repeat. Default is 0 (disabled) [ms]*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}repeat\PYGZus{}delay}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{delay}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*true (default): apply the start value immediately, false: apply start value after delay when the anim. really starts. */}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}set\PYGZus{}early\PYGZus{}apply}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nb}{false}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/* START THE ANIMATION}
\PYG{c+cm}{ *\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}anim\PYGZus{}start}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}                             \PYG{c+cm}{/*Start the animation*/}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can apply multiple different animations on the same variable at the same time.
For example, animate the x and y coordinates with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_x}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_y}}. However, only one animation can exist with a given variable and function pair and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_start()}} will remove any existing animations for such a pair.


\subsection{Animation path}
\label{\detokenize{overview/animation:animation-path}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can control the path of an animation. The most simple case is linear, meaning the current value between \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{end} is changed with fixed steps.
A \sphinxstyleemphasis{path} is a function which calculates the next value to set based on the current state of the animation. Currently, there are the following built\sphinxhyphen{}in path functions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_path\_linear}} linear animation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_path\_step}} change in one step at the end

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_path\_ease\_in}} slow at the beginning

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_path\_ease\_out}} slow at the end

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_path\_ease\_in\_out}} slow at the beginning and end

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_path\_overshoot}} overshoot the end value

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_path\_bounce}} bounce back a little from the end value (like hitting a wall)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Speed vs time}
\label{\detokenize{overview/animation:speed-vs-time}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, you set the animation time directly. But in some cases, setting the animation speed is more practical.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_speed\_to\_time(speed, start, end)}} function calculates the required time in milliseconds to reach the end value from a start value with the given speed.
The speed is interpreted in \sphinxstyleemphasis{unit/sec} dimension. For example,  \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_speed\_to\_time(20,0,100)}} will yield 5000 milliseconds. For example, in the case of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_set\_x}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{unit} is pixels so \sphinxstyleemphasis{20} means \sphinxstyleemphasis{20 px/sec} speed.


\subsection{Delete animations}
\label{\detokenize{overview/animation:delete-animations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can delete an animation with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_del(var, func)}} if you provide the animated variable and its animator function.


\subsection{Timeline}
\label{\detokenize{overview/animation:timeline}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A timeline is a collection of multiple animations which makes it easy to create complex composite animations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Firstly, create an animation element but don’t call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_start()}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Secondly, create an animation timeline object by calling \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_timeline\_create()}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thirdly, add animation elements to the animation timeline by calling \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_timeline\_add(at, start\_time, \&a)}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{start\_time}} is the start time of the animation on the timeline. Note that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{start\_time}} will override the value of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delay}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_timeline\_start(at)}} to start the animation timeline.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It supports forward and backward playback of the entire animation group, using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_timeline\_set\_reverse(at, reverse)}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_timeline\_stop(at)}} to stop the animation timeline.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_timeline\_set\_progress(at, progress)}} function to set the state of the object corresponding to the progress of the timeline.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_timeline\_get\_playtime(at)}} function to get the total duration of the entire animation timeline.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_timeline\_get\_reverse(at)}} function to get whether to reverse the animation timeline.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_anim\_timeline\_del(at)}} function to delete the animation timeline.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics{{anim-timeline}.png}

\label{\detokenize{overview/animation:examples}}

\section{Timers}
\label{\detokenize{overview/timer:timers}}\label{\detokenize{overview/timer::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LVGL has a built\sphinxhyphen{}in timer system. You can register a function to have it be called periodically. The timers are handled and called in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler()}}, which needs to be called every few milliseconds.
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{porting/timer-handler::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,doc,doc}{Porting}}}} for more information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Timers are non\sphinxhyphen{}preemptive, which means a timer cannot interrupt another timer. Therefore, you can call any LVGL related function in a timer.


\subsection{Create a timer}
\label{\detokenize{overview/timer:create-a-timer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To create a new timer, use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_create(timer\_cb, period\_ms, user\_data)}}. It will create an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_t *}} variable, which can be used later to modify the parameters of the timer.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_create\_basic()}} can also be used. This allows you to create a new timer without specifying any parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A timer callback should have a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void (*lv\_timer\_cb\_t)(lv\_timer\_t *);}} prototype.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{my\PYGZus{}timer}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}timer\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{timer}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Use the user\PYGZus{}data*/}
  \PYG{k+kt}{uint32\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{user\PYGZus{}data} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{timer}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{user\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{n}{printf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{my\PYGZus{}timer called with user data: \PYGZpc{}d}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{user\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Do something with LVGL*/}
  \PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{something\PYGZus{}happened}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{n}{something\PYGZus{}happened} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{false}\PYG{p}{;}
    \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}btn\PYGZus{}create}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}scr\PYGZus{}act}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
  \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}

\PYG{k}{static} \PYG{k+kt}{uint32\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{n}{user\PYGZus{}data} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}timer\PYGZus{}t} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{timer} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}timer\PYGZus{}create}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}timer}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{500}\PYG{p}{,}  \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{user\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Ready and Reset}
\label{\detokenize{overview/timer:ready-and-reset}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_ready(timer)}} makes a timer run on the next call of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler()}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_reset(timer)}} resets the period of a timer. It will be called again after the defined period of milliseconds has elapsed.


\subsection{Set parameters}
\label{\detokenize{overview/timer:set-parameters}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can modify some timer parameters later:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_set\_cb(timer, new\_cb)}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_set\_period(timer, new\_period)}}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Repeat count}
\label{\detokenize{overview/timer:repeat-count}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can make a timer repeat only a given number of times with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_set\_repeat\_count(timer, count)}}. The timer will automatically be deleted after it's called the defined number of times. Set the count to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}1}} to repeat indefinitely.


\subsection{Measure idle time}
\label{\detokenize{overview/timer:measure-idle-time}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can get the idle percentage time of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler}} with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_get\_idle()}}. Note that, it doesn't measure the idle time of the overall system, only \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler}}.
It can be misleading if you use an operating system and call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler}} in a timer, as it won't actually measure the time the OS spends in an idle thread.


\subsection{Asynchronous calls}
\label{\detokenize{overview/timer:asynchronous-calls}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In some cases, you can't perform an action immediately. For example, you can't delete an object because something else is still using it, or you don't want to block the execution now.
For these cases, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_async\_call(my\_function, data\_p)}} can be used to call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{my\_function}} on the next invocation of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data\_p}} will be passed to the function when it's called.
Note that only the data pointer is saved, so you need to ensure that the variable will be "alive" while the function is called. It can be \sphinxstyleemphasis{static}, global or dynamically allocated data.
If you want to cancel an asynchronous call, call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_async\_call\_cancel(my\_function, data\_p)}}, which will clear all asynchronous calls matching \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{my\_function}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data\_p}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{n+nf}{my\PYGZus{}screen\PYGZus{}clean\PYGZus{}up}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{scr}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Free some resources related to `scr`*/}

  \PYG{c+cm}{/*Finally delete the screen*/}
  \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}obj\PYGZus{}del}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{scr}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Do something with the object on the current screen*/}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*Delete screen on next call of `lv\PYGZus{}timer\PYGZus{}handler`, not right now.*/}
\PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}async\PYGZus{}call}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}screen\PYGZus{}clean\PYGZus{}up}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lv\PYGZus{}scr\PYGZus{}act}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cm}{/*The screen is still valid so you can do other things with it*/}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you just want to delete an object and don't need to clean anything up in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{my\_screen\_cleanup}} you could just use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_obj\_del\_async}} which will delete the object on the next call to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lv\_timer\_handler}}.


\subsection{API}
